title: Rethinking SAE Evaluation: An Atomic Interpretable Unit Framework Reveals Hidden Polysemanticity and Redundancy

paper.title: Rethinking SAE Evaluation: An Atomic Interpretable Unit Framework Reveals Hidden Polysemanticity and Redundancy
paper.abstract: Abstract Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) were originally motivated by discovering monosemantic features, a property that characterizes individual features but does not specify what the learned feature set should look like as a whole. As SAEs have increasingly been adopted for attribution, circuit discovery, and intervention, researchers have begun evaluating metrics that describe global properties of the feature set, such as sparsity, dead feature rates, reconstruction fidelity, and disentanglement, a diverse set that extends far beyond monosemanticity. However, this implicit shift beyond monosemanticity has not been formalized as a clear, well-defined objective that comes before these evaluation metrics. Without such an objective, existing metrics remain ad hoc, with their necessity unjustified. In this work, we formalize this ultimate objective by introducing a new paradigm for SAE evaluation: requiring that SAE features, and more generally dictionary-based decompositions of model representations, form an atomic interpretable unit basis, a coordinate system for semantically meaningful explanation. Under this paradigm, we organize existing and new measurements such as DAME (Dominance-Aware Monosemanticity Evaluation) as proxy metrics and introduce a comprehensive benchmarking framework. Evaluating hundreds of SAEs across multiple architectures and model families, we uncover failure modes in which some SAEs appear monosemantic under existing evaluation metrics while remaining functionally polysemantic: the most dominant features, those contributing most to model computation, are systematically less interpretable and more redundant. These failure modes warrant attention from SAE researchers as targets for improved training and architectures, and motivate dominance-aware evaluation as a standard check for practitioners before SAE features are deployed for attribution, circuit tracing, or intervention.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) entered mechanistic interpretability with a clear and well-motivated objective: addressing superposition by recovering monosemantic features ( Elhage et al., 2022 ) . Superposition arises when neural networks—particularly transformer-based language models—represent more meaningful concepts than they have activation dimensions, forcing multiple concepts to share the same representational space and rendering individual neurons polysemantic ( Elhage et al., 2022 ; Scherlis et al., 2022 ) . SAEs address this challenge by learning an expanded, sparse dictionary of feature directions. Concretely, they decompose a layer’s d in d_{\text{in}} -dimensional activations into m ≫ d in m\gg d_{\text{in}} learned features, with the goal that each feature corresponds to a single interpretable concept. Early work demonstrated that this sparsity-based dictionary learning approach can successfully disentangle superposed representations ( Sharkey et al., 2022 ; Cunningham et al., 2024 ; Bricken et al., 2023 ) , isolating coherent conceptual directions from an otherwise entangled activation space and offering a compelling solution to interpretability in large language models. As SAEs began to be used for LLM attribution, circuit discovery, and intervention ( Templeton et al., 2024 ; Marks et al., 2025 ; O’Neill and Bui, 2024 ) , researchers introduced diverse evaluation metrics: reconstruction fidelity, sparsity levels, dead feature rates, disentanglement, and intervention performance ( Gao et al., 2025 ; Rajamanoharan et al., 2024b ; Chanin et al., 2025 ) . Different works emphasized different subsets ( Bricken et al., 2023 ; Cunningham et al., 2024 ; Gao et al., 2025 ) , while benchmarking efforts like SAEBench ( Karvonen et al., 2025 ) organized them into systematic taxonomies containing eight diverse metrics spanning four capability categories (reconstruction, concept detection, interpretability, and feature disentanglement). Yet a foundational question remains unaddressed: what objective do these metrics collectively serve? When one of these proposed metrics degrades, the SAE is deemed deficient—but the underlying notion of quality remains undefined. Connections between metrics are unclear, and their necessity is justified only post hoc. This gap reflects a deeper issue: monosemanticity, the original objective proposed for SAEs, is insufficient. A feature is monosemantic if it activates on a single coherent concept rather than responding to multiple unrelated patterns. As a local property of individual features, monosemanticity has nothing to do with metrics like reconstruction fidelity or dead feature counts that concern the feature set globally . The proliferation of metrics reveals an implicit shift toward a global objective—but one that remains theoretically unclear and unspecified. Some works have begun to explicitly propose foundational criteria for what properties the feature set itself should possess, such as atomicity, uniqueness, stability, and completeness ( Leask et al., 2025 ; Bussmann et al., 2024b ; Ayonrinde et al., 2024 ) . However, these properties and metrics are typically invoked without justification for why this particular set is necessary and sufficient, and crucially, without first specifying what function SAE features are meant to serve —the underlying objective that would determine which properties matter and why, which in turn determines what metrics should be used to evaluate them. Appendix A provides a more detailed discussion of the history of SAEs and the evolution of SAE evaluation. (a) (b) Figure 1 : (a) Paradigm shift in SAE evaluation: from expecting isolated monosemantic features to requiring that features jointly form an atomic interpretable unit basis. Under the old paradigm, newly proposed metrics function as tweak-and-patch additions, analogous to epicycles. (b) Natural atomic units in vision vs. language. Pixel patches exhibit bounded interpretive ambiguity, while individual tokens are structurally overloaded with unrelated roles. In this work, we address this foundational gap by formalizing a new paradigm for SAE evaluation (Figure 1(a) ). We specify (1) the ultimate objective that SAE features should serve: forming an atomic interpretable unit (AIU) basis (Section 2 )—a coordinate system in which attribution and intervention are semantically meaningful. Under this paradigm, we derive (2) five necessary criteria for interpretable feature dictionaries—non-redundancy, completeness, monosemanticity, no dead units, and per-input sparsity—as direct consequences of the atomic interpretable unit objective (Section 2 ). Building on this theoretical foundation, we develop a comprehensive SAE-specific evaluation framework (Section 3 and Appendix D ) that reorganizes existing measurements and introduces (3) novel metrics—particularly DAME (Dominance-Aware Monosemanticity Evaluation) for assessing monosemanticity, and decoder-based redundancy metrics with theoretical and geometric justification for why non-redundancy should be enforced on decoder directions (Appendix I )—to operationalize these criteria at scale. Our newly proposed metrics expose (4) critical failure modes—SAEs that appear monosemantic under existing metrics while remaining functionally polysemantic due to dominance (a feature’s per-input fraction of total activation; Section 3.1 ) and redundancy (distinct features with near-identical decoder directions; Section 3.3 ) effects previously undetectable by prior evaluation schemes (Section 4 ). Beyond these core contributions, we also: (5) provide a comprehensive open-source benchmark (Appendix F ) across existing SAE families including SAEBench, JBloom, and CanRager, as well as (6) a large suite of newly trained SAE variants spanning multiple architectures and three different LLMs to systematically explore the hyperparameter space. Code is available at https://github.com/ritengzhang77-max/SAE-AIU and the checkpoints of our newly trained SAEs at https://huggingface.co/ritengzhang/SAE-AIU .

sections.heading: 2 The Atomic Interpretable Unit Framework
sections.text: Understanding how language models make decisions requires explanations that are both faithful (accurately reflecting internal computation) and human-understandable (expressed in meaningful terms). Modern attribution methods identify which units contribute to predictions, but they do not determine which units are appropriate to explain over . Faithful attribution over the wrong units yields explanations that are computationally faithful yet not meaningfully interpretable to humans. To formalize what makes attribution meaningful, we introduce two key objects:

sections.heading: Concepts ( 𝒞 \mathcal{C} ).
sections.text: The set of concepts we want to explain—objects, syntactic roles, semantic relationships, reasoning patterns, and other meaningful computational units that matter for understanding model behavior.

sections.heading: Interpretable units ( U U ).
sections.text: The units we actually attribute to during explanation. Each unit u ∈ U u\in U must be interpretable to humans and can relate to one or more concepts in 𝒞 \mathcal{C} . Unlike raw computational elements (individual pixels, tokens, or neuron activations), interpretable units are chosen specifically to support meaningful attribution. Here, an atomic explanatory unit is a basic coordinate to which attribution is assigned directly, without further decomposition within the chosen explanatory interface.

sections.heading: 2.1 Why Natural Coordinates Fail: Intuition
sections.text: For natural model coordinates, U U is formed from or composed of basic architectural elements. We can examine whether these natural choices of U U satisfy even the minimum injectivity requirement (Figure 1(b) ).

sections.heading: Vision: partial success.
sections.text: For traditional image models that don’t involve complex reasoning steps, we can take U U to be pixel patches. This approximately achieves 𝒞 → U \mathcal{C}\to U injectivity: visual concepts (objects, parts, textures) occupy compact, limited-overlapping spatial regions, so different concepts typically map to different patches. A pixel patch participates in only a few human-meaningful concepts; moreover, spatially coherent patches have bounded interpretive ambiguity . Given a patch that participates in a concept, a human observer can usually identify a small, tightly related set of plausible interpretations—e.g., a dog ear’s shape, color, texture, or the broader category “ear.” These alternatives are few and semantically coherent, so input patches can serve as useful interpretable units for visual attribution, even if they do not correspond perfectly to a single concept.

sections.heading: LLMs fail at input level.
sections.text: For language models, the natural choice is U U = token spans. However, tokens simultaneously participate in many unrelated conceptual roles spanning multiple levels of abstraction. Consider the token “Socrates” appearing in the syllogism: “Socrates is human; all humans are mortal; therefore Socrates is mortal.” Attribution to this token cannot distinguish whether the model is responding to its lexical identity, its role as a named entity, its function as a logical variable, its position as the subject of a premise, participation in a syllogistic reasoning pattern, or surface cues such as capitalization or sentence-initial position. These interpretations are not minor variants of the same concept but belong to fundamentally different conceptual categories. As a result, the mapping 𝒞 → U \mathcal{C}\to U is highly non-injective: many unrelated concepts collapse onto the same token, making attribution inherently ambiguous.

sections.heading: LLMs fail at activation level.
sections.text: At the activation level, we might take U U to be individual neurons or groups of neurons. However, language models exhibit superposition ( Elhage et al., 2022 ) : they represent far more features than activation dimensions. Each neuron or residual stream coordinate already mixes many unrelated internal features. Because of superposition, 𝒞 → U \mathcal{C}\to U fails injectivity: multiple distinct concepts are superposed onto the same neuron, so neuron-level attribution cannot meaningfully distinguish which concept is active.

sections.heading: The minimum requirement revealed.
sections.text: These failures across different choices of U U reveal a fundamental requirement: for attribution to be semantically meaningful, distinct concepts must map to distinct units—formally, the mapping 𝒞 → U \mathcal{C}\to U must be injective. Vision achieves this through spatial locality; LLMs fail because tokens participate in many overlapping concepts and neurons exhibit superposition. Without injectivity, when a unit activates, we cannot tell which concept is responsible, making attribution ambiguous.

The dictionary size m ≫ d in m\gg d_{\text{in}} allows the SAE to represent more features than the original activation dimension.

sections.heading: The key distinction.
sections.text: For natural coordinates (tokens, neurons, pixel patches), U U is fixed by the model architecture, composed from its basic elements; we can only hope for partial coverage of 𝒞 \mathcal{C} and must work with whatever U U the architecture provides. For SAE features, U U is learned from scratch to be a concept set, not constrained by architectural choices, and we control | U | = m |U|=m (the number of features). Each SAE feature is a candidate atomic unit: f i ​ ( x ) f_{i}(x) measures how much the unit is used on input x x , while the decoder direction d i d_{i} specifies what it represents (the vector it writes into the residual stream). Thus SAEs provide an interpretability interface by mapping raw activations to feature coordinates f ⁡ ( x ) f(x) on which attribution can be performed directly.

sections.heading: 2.3 What Makes Good Atomic Units?
sections.text: Given this key distinction—that SAEs explicitly construct U U to approximate 𝒞 \mathcal{C} —the goal for SAE features is not merely to function as an atomic interpretable unit basis, but to directly learn features that approximate a meaningful concept set. Table 1 summarizes the criteria.

sections.heading: The one-to-one ideal.
sections.text: Ideally, features and concepts should be in one-to-one correspondence. This requires two conditions: each feature represents one concept ⇒ \Rightarrow monosemanticity (C3): features shouldn’t mix unrelated concepts; and each concept has one feature ⇒ \Rightarrow non-redundancy (C1): features shouldn’t duplicate representations.

sections.heading: The granularity problem.
sections.text: Even with one-to-one correspondence, the SAE must learn features at the right level of detail. Let m m denote the number of learned features and let n ideal n_{\mathrm{ideal}} denote the appropriate number of concepts for this layer. If m < n ideal m<n_{\mathrm{ideal}} , the SAE recovers too few concepts: without enforcing surjectivity U → 𝒞 U\to\mathcal{C} , this causes incompleteness (C2)—some meaningful concepts remain unrecovered—while forcing surjectivity requires units to cover multiple concepts, breaking monosemanticity (C3). If m > n ideal m>n_{\mathrm{ideal}} , the SAE learns too many features: without forcing surjectivity 𝒞 → U \mathcal{C}\to U , this creates dead features (violating C4)—units that never activate meaningfully—while forcing surjectivity requires multiple features to map to the same concept, breaking non-redundancy (C1).

sections.heading: Sparsity: cognitive accessibility.
sections.text: Even with correct feature-concept correspondence at appropriate granularity, explanations are only human-usable when few features activate per input. C1–C4 constrain semantic correspondence between concepts and units, whereas C5 independently constrains the number of units participating in a particular explanation: a dictionary could have a clean one-to-one concept–unit correspondence yet activate thousands of individually meaningful features on one input, and a thousand-term attribution would not be cognitively usable. C5 therefore follows from the human-usable part of the AIU objective rather than from the correspondence mapping. Per-input sparsity (C5) ensures that ‖ f ⁡ ( x ) ‖ 0 ≤ k \|f(x)\|_{0}\leq k for small k k , making explanations cognitively accessible.

sections.heading: Checkable evidence for C3.
sections.text: C3 is the injectivity condition 𝒞 → U \mathcal{C}\to U for a target concept set fixed at a stated explanatory granularity. With ground-truth concept–unit relations, as in a synthetic or supervised setting, it can be checked directly; for open-ended LLM representations neither 𝒞 \mathcal{C} nor the concept–unit relation is exhaustively observed, so auto-interpretability methods instead provide checkable behavioral evidence relevant to C3: whether a proposed explanation predicts held-out feature behavior beyond an uninformative baseline (Appendix D.3 ). This evidence depends on the chosen concept granularity, evaluation distribution, explainer, and evaluator. sections.heading: 3 Evaluating the Five Criteria for SAE
sections.text: The five criteria from Section 2 establish necessary conditions for SAE features to function as an atomic interpretable unit basis. These conditions are necessary rather than sufficient for causal use, which additionally depends on whether and how features are recruited by downstream layers’ computation under a particular context, intervention, and outcome. However, these criteria were derived at the conceptual level---describing what properties the feature set must satisfy---without specifying how to operationalize them as concrete measurements in the SAE context. 1 1 1 Many existing SAE evaluation metrics act as joint proxies for multiple criteria out of the five; a detailed correlation study and per-evaluation mapping (covering Sparse Probing, SCR, TPP, Feature Absorption, RAVEL, and Unlearning from SAEBench ( Karvonen et al., 2025 ) ) is provided in Appendix D.6 . For C2 (Completeness) , C4 (No dead units) , and C5 (Per-input sparsity) , certain standard proxy metrics from prior work map naturally to our framework: for example, reconstruction fidelity metrics for completeness; firing frequency statistics for dead units; and mean L 0 L_{0} (the number of features active on an input) for sparsity. We adopt these established measurements in our benchmarking with one addition: an effective sparsity metric that accounts for activation magnitude distribution (detailed in Appendix D ).

sections.heading: 3.1 The Local-to-Global Aggregation Problem for C1/C3
sections.text: The remaining two criteria— C1 (Non-redundancy) and C3 (Monosemanticity) —present a qualitatively different measurement challenge. Unlike C2/C4/C5 , which admit direct dictionary-level proxy measurements , C1/C3 are defined as local properties : monosemanticity is a property of individual features, while non-redundancy is a property of feature pairs. Consequently, determining whether an SAE satisfies C1/C3 as global requirements for an atomic interpretable unit basis demands an explicit local-to-global aggregation principle . Yet most existing SAE evaluations effectively assume one by default: they aggregate local measurements across features (or feature pairs) using uniform weighting to produce a single dictionary-level score. This assumption is fragile because feature usage is highly imbalanced: a small subset of units accounts for a disproportionate share of activation (and therefore attribution), and thus disproportionately influences SAE-based interpretability analyses (e.g., circuit tracing); their quality should therefore be weighted more heavily. We stratify features by mean dominance , ρ ¯ i = 𝔼 x ​ [ ρ i ​ ( x ) ] \bar{\rho}_{i}=\mathbb{E}_{x}[\rho_{i}(x)] , where ρ i ​ ( x ) = | f i ​ ( x ) | / ∑ j = 1 m | f j ​ ( x ) | \rho_{i}(x)=|f_{i}(x)|/\sum_{j=1}^{m}|f_{j}(x)| is the fraction of total activation contributed by feature i i on input x x . When a non-atomic feature accounts for a large share of a representation, misinterpreting it distorts a large portion of what the SAE represents at that input. Complementary firing-frequency and activation-magnitude analyses, including their definitions and distinction from mean dominance, are in Appendix G . Figure 2 shows that even in SAEs with thousands of features (4,000–128,000), the 10 most frequently firing features contribute a median of 7.8% of per-input activation; the top-30 distribution (median 13.0%) is in Appendix G (Figure 34 ). Remarkably, higher sparsity (lower L 0 L_{0} ) correlates with higher dominance across all evaluated SAE families—e.g., in GPT2-Small SAEs (where all SAE architectures show the trend), 94% of width-architecture combinations (17 of 18) show positive correlations (Appendix G ). This raises a fundamental open question: whether increasing sparsity constraints truly decompose features into finer-grained atomic units, or instead primarily reduce sparsity loss by suppressing non-dominant features while concentrating computation into a smaller set of increasingly dominant ones.

sections.heading: 3.2 C3: Monosemanticity—DAME
sections.text: Monosemanticity concerns whether inputs with sufficiently large activation (e.g., { x : | f i ​ ( x ) | ≥ ϵ } \{x:|f_{i}(x)|\geq\epsilon\} ) share a coherent semantic property. In practice, this is assessed using the standard auto-interpretability pipeline ( Bills et al., 2023 ) , which proceeds in two stages. First, for each feature i i , an LLM (the explainer ) is shown a small set of high activation examples and produces a natural-language explanation describing the feature’s firing behavior. Second, the proposed explanation is evaluated on held-out validation inputs S i S_{i} using an LLM-based judge: the judge predicts the feature’s activation behavior, with labels derived from the precomputed activations f i ​ ( x ) f_{i}(x) for x ∈ S i x\in S_{i} .

sections.heading: Validation framing.
sections.text: Prior approaches frame validation in ways that fail to test whether explanations can distinguish high from low activation, particularly under severe feature firing frequency imbalance. Binary classification asks whether a feature fired or not ( Paulo et al., 2024 ) . However, if a rare feature never receives a positive example during validation, the explanation cannot be tested at all. For instance, suppose a polysemantic feature i i truly activates on two unrelated but rare triggers—mentions of Socrates and mentions of Los Angeles —so that f i ​ ( x ) > 0 f_{i}(x)>0 on only ∼ \sim 0.01% of tokens. If S i S_{i} is sampled uniformly at random from the corpus, it is likely that no input in S i S_{i} contains either trigger, yielding an all-negative validation set. In that case, any explanation (even an incorrect one that only describes “Socrates” and ignores “Los Angeles”) will appear to achieve perfect accuracy simply by always predicting “does not fire.” The same issue applies symmetrically to high-frequency features: when a feature fires nearly 100% of the time, negative examples become impossible to sample, so false positives cannot be detected. Discretized magnitude prediction bins activations into fixed intervals (e.g., 10 bins) normalized by each feature’s maximum activation ( Bills et al., 2023 ) . This remains problematic: when features exhibit outliers, the maximum activation skews the bin boundaries, compressing inputs with meaningfully different activation magnitudes into the same label. Important distinctions go untested.

sections.heading: DAME.
sections.text: We propose Dominance-Aware Monosemanticity Evaluation (DAME), which addresses both challenges: 1. Dominance-stratified feature sampling. To address the dominance weighting problem, we rank features by mean dominance ρ ¯ i \bar{\rho}_{i} and sample from each dominance quantile separately, ensuring evaluation coverage across the full dominance spectrum. Dominance is used for stratified sampling and aggregation; it is not an input to any feature’s score. 2. Activation-balanced contrastive validation. For each feature, we bin all inputs into three groups (low, medium, high activation) based on that feature’s own activation distribution using quantile splits. Each validation question presents one example from each bin, without showing activation values, and asks the LLM to rank the three examples by activation strength given only the explanation, guaranteeing adaptive coverage across the full activation spectrum within every validation question. We score each feature by perfect ranking accuracy : the fraction of validation questions for which the LLM predicts the exact activation order (Appendix D.3.1 ). In a controlled test of high-versus-middle activation reversals that preserve binary firing support, DAME ranks the correct explanation above the reversed one for all 80 synthetic features, compared with 67 for discretized magnitude and at most 22 for binary/fuzz-style scoring (Appendix J.1 ).

sections.heading: 3.3 C1: Non-Redundancy—Decoder Cosine Similarity
sections.text: Non-redundancy requires that distinct features encode distinct concepts. Though not often evaluated, when researchers do measure redundancy ( Karvonen et al., 2025 ) , they use decoder cosine similarity, sim ​ ( i , j ) = d i ⋅ d j ‖ d i ‖ ​ ‖ d j ‖ \text{sim}(i,j)=\frac{d_{i}\cdot d_{j}}{\|d_{i}\|\|d_{j}\|} . However, this decoder-side measure is adopted without explaining why decoder redundancy (rather than encoder redundancy) is the appropriate notion for C1. We provide a justification below and report per-quantile decoder cosine similarity in Section 4 . Encoder-decoder asymmetry. Each encoder weight vector w i w_{i} (the i i -th row of W W ) functions as a sparse classifier that carves out a small firing region in activation space. Because of the per-input sparsity constraint, most features must fire on only a tiny fraction of inputs. However, transformer activations cluster near a dominant mean direction (Appendix Figure 41 ), causing encoder weights to be almost orthogonal to this mean (typically near 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} ; Appendix Figure 46 ). If w i w_{i} were close to the mean input direction (say, within 40 ∘ 40^{\circ} ), the feature would activate on nearly all inputs, violating sparsity. Thus encoder directions cannot reliably align with semantic features. This encoder–decoder angular mismatch is natural and benign (Appendix Figure 43 ): the encoder w i w_{i} specifies a decision boundary that controls when a feature fires, while the decoder d i d_{i} specifies the concept—the semantic direction it writes. Sparsity eliminates encoder redundancy. Moreover, sparsity constraints already regulate encoder-side redundancy. If two features have w i ≈ w j w_{i}\approx w_{j} , they fire on the same inputs with the same magnitude, so the SAE can merge them into a single feature with decoder d i + d j d_{i}+d_{j} , achieving identical reconstruction while reducing the sparsity penalty. Decoder redundancy, however, is not directly penalized by the standard SAE objective (reconstruction plus sparsity), and can therefore persist. Empirical validation of the proxy. We additionally verify that decoder cosine similarity tracks semantic alignment: computing per-feature explanation embeddings, mean embedding similarity rises monotonically with decoder cosine similarity (pooled Spearman r s = 0.42 r_{s}{=}0.42 , p < 10 − 10 p{<}10^{-10} ); details in Appendix D.1.1 .

sections.heading: 4 Results
sections.text: We evaluated 600+ SAEs across 7 SAE families (Appendix C ; 28,000+ features sampled). Our findings reveal that dominant features—those contributing most to model computation—are systematically less monosemantic and more redundant (detailed benchmark results for all five AIU criteria in Appendix F ). In this section, for both monosemanticity and redundancy metrics, we report results across four dominance quantiles (Q1–Q4), where Q1 contains the most dominant features (highest mean dominance ρ ¯ i \bar{\rho}_{i} ) and Q4 the least.

sections.heading: 4.1 Dominant Features Show Lower Monosemanticity
sections.text: Across all SAEs evaluated with our DAME framework, top-quartile (Q1) features have systematically lower monosemanticity than the rest of the dictionary (Q2–Q4). The effect is statistically significant at the per-SAE level (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: p = 6.76 × 10 − 8 p=6.76\times 10^{-8} , Cohen’s d = − 0.278 d=-0.278 ). We count an SAE as having a Q1 deficit when its mean perfect ranking accuracy is lower for Q1 than for Q2–Q4; 65.2% of SAEs individually show a Q1 deficit. On average across all evaluated SAEs (per-SAE mean), Q1 features achieve 61.8% perfect ranking accuracy compared to 64.1% for Q2–Q4. This inverse relationship between dominance and monosemanticity—where the most computationally important features are the least monosemantic—directly contradicts the expectation that dominant features should be monosemantic. Across 210 synthetic SAEs at widths 128–1024, Q1 features show lower prevalence-corrected held-out support containment than Q2–Q4 overall (one-sided SAE-level sign test, p = 1.6 × 10 − 12 p=1.6\times 10^{-12} ; Appendix J.6 ). This measures whether a feature fires within a single concept without penalizing incomplete concept coverage. A complementary correlation-gap analysis finds a significant Q1 deficit in 71 of 105 SAEs (Appendix D.3.2 ).

sections.heading: Dominant features concentrate redundancy.
sections.text: We report redundancy at a primary decoder cosine threshold of 0.7 and test robustness across thresholds of 0.6–0.9 (Figure 4 a). We use full-dictionary dominance quartiles and remove pairs involving features that never fire in the evaluation sample, applying the same rule to all four groups. To account for unequal group sizes after filtering, we normalize each quartile’s share of redundant-edge endpoints by its share of active features. This endpoint enrichment equivalently compares the group’s mean number of redundant connections per feature with the mean across all active features; Q1 enrichment above 1 × 1\times therefore implies a higher mean than Q2–Q4 combined. On the complete graph, including cross-quartile pairs, the median Q1 enrichment is 1.64 × 1.64\times (95% SAE-bootstrap CI 1.51–1.74), with 71.5% of SAEs above the 1 × 1\times null. Within-quartile-only results and per-architecture breakdowns are in Appendix F.4 . The most dominant features are especially affected: for Standard ReLU SAEs, 26.1% of top-10 features participate in Q1 redundant pairs, with 4.7 pairs forming within the top-10 alone (Appendix Table 16 ); 20.5% of top-100 features are involved in Q1 redundant pairs, with 296.3 pairs forming within the top-100 (Appendix Table 19 ). Figure 4 : Redundancy among dominant features. (a) Q1 endpoint enrichment among redundant edges as a function of the decoder cosine similarity threshold (full-dictionary dominance quartiles, symmetric active-only filter): median over SAEs for each architecture; the dashed line is the median over all SAEs with its 95% SAE-bootstrap confidence interval and the dotted line is the 1 × 1\times null. (b) Mean encoder similarity over all feature pairs by dominance quartile.

sections.heading: Redundant features differ in encoder direction.
sections.text: Q1 features exhibit the lowest encoder similarity (mean: 0.056) compared to Q2–Q4 (0.109–0.135) (Figure 4 b; Appendix Table 20 ). Critically, this pattern persists even among redundant pairs: Q1 redundant pairs have encoder similarity of 0.428 versus 0.661 for Q2–Q4 redundant pairs. Decoder-aligned pairs can therefore have dissimilar encoders; whether their firing supports are complementary must be assessed from activation data.

sections.heading: The feature sharding failure mode.
sections.text: We use feature sharding to describe a pairwise representational pattern in which features share (nearly) the same decoder direction d i ≈ d j d_{i}\approx d_{j} , have dissimilar encoders w i ≉ w j w_{i}\not\approx w_{j} , and fire on complementary regions of activation space while writing the same semantic direction. Feature sharding can preserve reconstruction fidelity and per-input sparsity while reducing dead features, and may therefore be favored by objectives with explicit dead-feature penalties. An SAE can thus appear healthy under common diagnostics even as its effective semantic dictionary collapses to far fewer directions. Concretely, consider a semantic direction encoding the concept of color . Rather than learning a single feature that activates whenever color is relevant, an SAE may shard this direction into multiple features whose encoders gate activation on additional, unrelated contextual factors (e.g., gendered language, syntactic role, or discourse position), effectively learning features of the form color ∧ \wedge context . During attribution, whenever color contributes to the model’s computation, exactly one such shard fires—maintaining sparsity—so attribution is tied to the shard’s gating context rather than to the underlying concept of color itself.

sections.heading: A functional sharding example.
sections.text: In a TopK-65k SAE trained on Pythia-160M, feature 41902 activates on definite-article contexts ( the / The ), whereas feature 46571 activates on possessive/genitive-determiner contexts ( its , his , their , whose , and possessive ’s ). Their encoder and decoder cosine similarities are 0.2066 and 0.7405, respectively. Their natural supports are largely separated under the SAE’s exact TopK gate: 316 versus 57 firings, only 7 co-firings, and Jaccard 0.019. On an independent fixed target-prompt family, we injected equal- L 2 L_{2} decoder directions only at positions where both native TopK gates were naturally inactive (18/20 prompts); protocol in Appendix J.9 . Both writes increased the fixed target token aim in the actual downstream forward pass: mean logit changes were + 0.556 +0.556 and + 0.611 +0.611 , with 15/18 and 16/18 positive prompt-level effects. The induced effect vectors had cosine 0.943 (relative to support-size- and decoder-norm-matched low-decoder-similarity controls, the mean candidate-pair advantage was + 0.472 +0.472 logit; bootstrap 95% CI [ + 0.347 , + 0.597 ] [+0.347,+0.597] ). Together, the separated natural supports and aligned intervention effects provide a functional sharding case: the two features specialize to different determiner contexts while producing similar downstream decoder writes. Sharding differs from feature absorption ( Chanin et al., 2025 ) , in which a general-concept feature fails to activate on more specific cases while other features take over its role; the two can coexist. In terms of firing positions, sharding corresponds to decoder-aligned features that fire at largely separate positions, whereas absorption is compatible with one feature’s firing positions being largely contained within the other’s. In a broader analysis of decoder-aligned pairs, 21.5% fire at largely separate positions and in 15.3% one feature’s firing positions are largely contained within the other’s (equal-weight means of within-SAE percentages; Appendix J.11 ).

sections.heading: 5 Discussion
sections.text: Our findings reveal three recurring correlated phenomena: (1) higher sparsity often correlates with higher dominance concentration (Section 3.1 ), (2) dominant features show lower monosemanticity (Section 4.1 ), and (3) dominant features exhibit more redundancy (Section 4.2 ). The case study also illustrates feature sharding , in which features fire in distinct contexts but produce similar decoder writes. Together, these suggest sparsity constraints in SAE training may be satisfied in ways that do not improve interpretability: dominant features either remain polysemantic or are duplicated across features with similar decoder directions—both allow SAEs to meet sparsity and dead features penalties while leaving the most computationally important structure entangled, raising concerns for SAE-based attribution and circuit tracing.

sections.heading: Recommendations for practitioners and researchers.
sections.text: For these reasons, before SAE features are deployed for attribution, circuit tracing, or intervention, we recommend dominance-stratified evaluation as a standard check: (1) monosemanticity across dominance quantiles, and (2) decoder similarity among high-dominance features. These failure modes also warrant attention from SAE researchers as targets for improved training objectives and architectures that reduce polysemanticity and redundancy in high-dominance features. Limitations of the present work are discussed in Appendix B .

sections.heading: Appendix A Extended Related Work
sections.text: This appendix discusses related work along the three threads that frame our contribution: (i) sparse autoencoders for mechanistic interpretability, (ii) SAE evaluation metrics and benchmarking, and (iii) feature-set desiderata.

sections.heading: A.1 Sparse Autoencoders for Mechanistic Interpretability
sections.text: Sparse autoencoders address superposition [ Elhage et al., 2022 ] by learning overcomplete sparse dictionaries that isolate monosemantic features [ Sharkey et al., 2022 , Cunningham et al., 2024 , Bricken et al., 2023 , Templeton et al., 2024 ] . Numerous architectural variants have improved reconstruction fidelity through different sparsity mechanisms [ Gao et al., 2025 , Rajamanoharan et al., 2024b , Rajamanoharan et al., 2024a , Bussmann et al., 2024a , Karvonen et al., 2024b , Ayonrinde, 2024 , Bussmann et al., 2025 ] , while alternative approaches explore different training objectives such as transcoders [ Paulo et al., 2025 , Dunefsky et al., 2024 ] , crosscoders [ Lindsey et al., 2024 ] , and end-to-end sparse dictionary learning [ Braun et al., 2024 ] .

sections.heading: A.2 SAE Evaluation Metrics and Benchmarking
sections.text: SAE evaluation initially focused on the foundational goal of monosemanticity. Bills et al. [2023] introduced automated interpretability scoring, using language models to assess whether individual features respond to coherent, singular concepts based on their activation patterns across input sequences. Basic sanity checks measured necessary conditions for SAE quality: reconstruction fidelity (MSE, loss recovered) [ Bricken et al., 2023 , Cunningham et al., 2024 ] —if an SAE cannot faithfully reconstruct activations, it cannot be a good decomposition—and sparsity (L0 norm) [ Bricken et al., 2023 , Cunningham et al., 2024 ] —high per-input activation counts can make an attribution difficult to inspect even when individual features are monosemantic. Additionally, dead feature rates [ Bricken et al., 2023 , Templeton et al., 2024 ] track features that rarely activate, indicating wasted capacity. Multiple early works [ Bricken et al., 2023 , Cunningham et al., 2024 , Bills et al., 2023 ] extended evaluation to measure whether SAEs preserve model performance when their reconstructions replace original activations, testing reconstruction fidelity via downstream loss (cross-entropy, KL divergence). Karvonen et al. [2025] systematized evaluation with SAEBench, a comprehensive benchmark spanning reconstruction, interpretability (automated interpretability scoring), disentanglement, and concept detection metrics [ Chanin et al., 2025 ] .

sections.heading: A.3 Feature Set Desiderata
sections.text: The lack of ground-truth features for comparison [ Makelov et al., 2024 ] led researchers to develop supervised evaluation methods using tasks with known feature structure [ Gurnee et al., 2023 , Gao et al., 2025 , Huang et al., 2024 , Marks et al., 2025 , Farrell et al., 2024 , Karvonen et al., 2024a , Karvonen et al., 2024b , Venhoff et al., 2024 , Karvonen et al., 2025 ] . However, numerous works found that SAE features underperform compared to supervised methods on these supervised tasks [ Kantamneni et al., 2025 , Wu et al., 2025 , Smith et al., 2025 ] . Peng et al. [2026] reframed these negative results by distinguishing SAE objectives: even if SAEs underperform on pre-specified supervised tasks, they excel at discovering unknown concepts [ Movva et al., 2025 ] and enabling circuit discovery [ Marks et al., 2025 , O’Neill and Bui, 2024 , Ameisen et al., 2025 , Lindsey et al., 2025 , Lindsey et al., 2024 ] . To evaluate such learned unknown feature sets, some researchers addressed pathological behaviors including feature suppression [ Wright and Sharkey, 2024 ] , feature absorption [ Chanin et al., 2025 ] , feature splitting [ Bricken et al., 2023 ] , and redundancy [ Karvonen et al., 2025 ] , while others raised stability concerns— Paulo and Belrose [2025] found only 30% feature sharing across random seeds. Leask et al. [2025] examined whether SAEs find “canonical units of analysis,” defining such a set as simultaneously unique (no variations across runs), complete (encompassing all necessary features), and atomic (indivisible), finding evidence against all three through SAE stitching and meta-SAEs. While these properties and failure modes have been proposed and discussed, they lack derivation from a principled objective specifying what function SAE features should serve [ Sharkey et al., 2025 ] —a gap our framework fills.

sections.heading: Appendix B Limitations
sections.text: We highlight several limitations of the present work.

sections.heading: Model-scale coverage.
sections.text: The primary benchmark uses models in the 70M–2.7B parameter range (TinyStories, Pythia-70M / 160M, GPT-2-Small, OPT-125M, and Gemma-2-2B). Additional public-SAE evaluations on Qwen3-8B / 14B / 32B and Gemma-2-9B extend the observed scope of the Q1 token-DAME deficit (Appendix J.10 ), but cover limited model, layer, and SAE-family combinations. These checks do not establish scale invariance, a monotonic scaling trend, or larger-model replication of every failure mode, including redundancy. The contribution is the framework itself; broader scaling behavior remains open.

sections.heading: Proxy nature of monosemanticity scoring.
sections.text: Any monosemanticity metric that uses an LLM as a judge—including the auto-interpretability scores of Bills et al. [2023] and Paulo et al. [2024] , the SAEBench AutoInterp evaluation, and our DAME—inherits a shared limitation: the judge can itself produce noisy or polysemantic explanations, and its scores are bounded by the judging LLM’s own representational fidelity for the concepts it is asked to label. DAME does not escape this limitation; its contribution is dominance-aware stratification of the same proxy, not a replacement of LLM-based judging. Improvements to the judging LLM, the prompting strategy, or the validation question construction would change all such metrics’ absolute numbers in correlated ways. We expect the relative ordering across SAEs and across dominance quantiles to be more robust than the absolute values, but this is itself a proxy property and the limitation should be acknowledged.

sections.heading: Ground-truth concept sets are conditional, not unobtainable.
sections.text: A common framing of SAE evaluation is that “ground-truth concepts are unavailable for real LLMs.” The situation is more nuanced: a ground-truth concept set can in principle be inferred for a real LLM, but only conditional on (i) the chosen SAE width m m being close to the true cardinality of the underlying concept set, and (ii) the granularity of the discovered features lying within a range that humans can verify. Both conditions are difficult to certify for any individual SAE, which is why we rely on proxy metrics that provide empirical evidence relevant to the AIU criteria. Our synthetic validation (Appendix D.3.2 ) sidesteps both conditions by constructing the concept set itself; the limitation is therefore not that ground truth is intrinsically unavailable, but that recovering it for a real LLM requires assumptions we have not yet verified.

sections.heading: Hyperparameter transfer and sparsity grid coverage.
sections.text: For the SAEs we trained ourselves we adopted hyperparameters from SAEBench’s Pythia and Gemma configurations as a starting point (Appendix F.2.1 ). This choice yields a wide divergence in effective sparsity across architectures: top- k k variants enforce a target L 0 L_{0} by construction, while Gated and JumpReLU rely on a soft penalty that does not transfer cleanly to LLMs of different scales and activation distributions. A more comprehensive per-LLM hyperparameter sweep, targeting comparable effective L 0 L_{0} across architectures, would likely sharpen and possibly reverse some of the architecture-specific patterns we report (the synthetic validation in Appendix D.3.2 , which controls sparsity directly during training, illustrates this: JumpReLU shows the strongest Q1 deficit on synthetic data even though it is non-significant on the real-LLM SAEs we train with our default hyperparameters).

sections.heading: Appendix C Experiment Details
sections.text: This appendix provides comprehensive details on our benchmarking experiments, covering the SAE families evaluated, their configurations, and the experimental setup. Our evaluation follows the Atomic Interpretable Unit (AIU) framework introduced in Section 2 , which establishes five necessary criteria for interpretable feature dictionaries: C1 (Non-redundancy) , C2 (Completeness) , C3 (Monosemanticity) , C4 (No dead units) , and C5 (Per-input sparsity) . We benchmark SAEs using both existing proxy metrics from prior work and newly proposed metrics that operationalize these criteria, as introduced in Section 3 . Comprehensive implementation details for all metrics and evaluation methodology are provided in Appendix D . Detailed benchmarking results across all evaluated SAEs are presented in Appendix F .

sections.heading: Appendix D Proxy Metrics for the Five AIU Criteria
sections.text: This appendix details the proxy metrics we employ to operationalize each of the five AIU criteria introduced in Section 2 . Since we do not assume access to a predefined concept set as ground truth, these metrics serve as practical proxies for evaluating whether SAE features form an atomic interpretable unit basis. We organize our discussion by criterion, describing what each metric measures, which ones we include, and relevant implementation details.

sections.heading: D.1 Proxy Metrics for Non-Redundancy (C1)
sections.text: For C1 (Non-redundancy) , we employ dominance-aware redundancy metrics that evaluate whether distinct features encode distinct concepts. The standard approach aggregates redundancy by uniformly counting redundant pairs: RedundancyRate θ = 1 ( m 2 ) ∑ i < j 𝟏 [ cos ( d i , d j ) ≥ θ ] \text{RedundancyRate}_{\theta}=\frac{1}{\binom{m}{2}}\sum_{i<j}\mathbf{1}[\cos(d_{i},d_{j})\geq\theta] . However, uniform aggregation ignores that redundancy among dominant features is far more problematic than redundancy among rare features. Our dominance-aware approach includes the top- n n dominance redundancy rate , which restricts evaluation to pairs among the n n most dominant features (selected by mean dominance ρ ¯ i \bar{\rho}_{i} ). Additional variants, including quantile-based redundancy metrics, are detailed in Section 3 and used in our evaluation. We evaluate redundancy using decoder cosine similarity, formally justified in Section 3.3 on the grounds that encoders act as gating mechanisms while decoders define semantic content. We compute decoder cosine similarity as sim ​ ( i , j ) = d i ⋅ d j ‖ d i ‖ ​ ‖ d j ‖ \text{sim}(i,j)=\frac{d_{i}\cdot d_{j}}{\|d_{i}\|\|d_{j}\|} for all feature pairs, where d i d_{i} and d j d_{j} are the decoder weight vectors. Features are ranked by mean dominance ρ ¯ i \bar{\rho}_{i} and split into four quantiles (Q1–Q4), where Q1 contains the most dominant features. We count redundant pairs as those with decoder cosine similarity ≥ 0.7 \geq 0.7 (following Karvonen et al. [2025] ) and report redundancy rates per quantile. We also compute encoder similarity among redundant features for comparison (Section 4.2 ).

sections.heading: D.1.1 Empirical Validation: Decoder Cosine Similarity vs. Semantic Alignment
sections.text: Section 3.3 provides a geometric argument for measuring redundancy on the decoder side. Here we additionally verify that decoder cosine similarity tracks semantic alignment between features—i.e., that the geometric proxy reflects what the features actually encode in concept space.

sections.heading: Workflow.
sections.text: For every SAE in our benchmark, we (1) collect the top-activating contexts for each feature (window sizes T ∈ { 8 , 16 , 32 , 64 } T\in\{8,16,32,64\} tokens around the maximum-activation position); (2) generate a natural-language explanation for each feature using an LLM (autointerp pipeline); (3) embed each explanation with sentence-BERT to obtain a feature-level explanation embedding e i ∈ ℝ 384 e_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{384} ; (4) for every feature pair ( i , j ) (i,j) with sufficiently distinct decoder directions, compute the pair-level explanation similarity cos ⁡ ( e i , e j ) \cos(e_{i},e_{j}) ; (5) aggregate by binning pairs by decoder cosine similarity and computing mean explanation similarity per bin.

sections.heading: Coverage.
sections.text: 136 SAEs across 5 LLM families (Gemma-2-2b, Pythia-160M, Pythia-70M via CanRager, GPT-2-small via JBloom and our training, and our training on OPT-125M and TinyStories) and 7 architectures (Standard, TopK, BatchTopK, Matryoshka, JumpReLU, Gated, PAnneal). At T = 8 T{=}8 , this yields 95,206 feature pairs.

sections.heading: Pooled result.
sections.text: Mean explanation similarity rises monotonically with decoder cosine similarity (Figure 5 , panel 5(a) ). Pooled Spearman r s = 0.42 r_{s}=0.42 at T = 8 T{=}8 , p < 10 − 10 p<10^{-10} . The trend is visually clear: pairs with decoder cosine ≥ 0.7 \geq 0.7 (our redundancy threshold) show explanation cosine substantially higher than pairs with decoder cosine ≤ 0.3 \leq 0.3 .

sections.text: The effect is not driven by a few outlier SAEs. Per-SAE Spearman correlations (Figure 5 , panel 5(b) ): 130 of 136 SAEs (96%) show positive correlation; median per-SAE r s ≈ 0.43 r_{s}\approx 0.43 . All per-LLM and per-architecture pools are statistically significant at p < 2.4 × 10 − 5 p<2.4\times 10^{-5} .

sections.text: Repeating the analysis at T ∈ { 8 , 16 , 32 , 64 } T\in\{8,16,32,64\} tokens yields qualitatively identical pooled trends, indicating the relationship is not an artifact of the specific window choice.

sections.text: Decoder cosine similarity is therefore a defensible proxy for semantic alignment: it geometrically measures direction overlap in the residual stream, and empirically that overlap predicts independent semantic similarity (estimated from explanations produced by an LLM). Pairs that the redundancy metric flags as redundant ( cos ≥ 0.7 \cos\geq 0.7 ) are also pairs that an external interpretability pipeline considers semantically alike. sections.heading: D.2 Proxy Metrics for Completeness (C2)
sections.text: For C2 (Completeness) , we evaluate how well SAE reconstructions capture the original activation space. Since we lack a predefined concept set as ground truth, the best we can do is use reconstruction fidelity and SAE training quality to estimate completeness—if an SAE cannot faithfully reconstruct activations, it cannot form a complete basis for semantic explanation. We employ three standard metrics that have become established in SAE evaluation:

sections.heading: Mean Squared Error (MSE).
sections.text: The most direct measure of reconstruction fidelity, MSE computes the average squared error between original activations ϕ ⁡ ( x ) \phi(x) and their reconstructions ϕ ^ ​ ( x ) \hat{\phi}(x) : MSE = 𝔼 x ​ [ ‖ ϕ ⁡ ( x ) − ϕ ^ ​ ( x ) ‖ 2 ] \text{MSE}=\mathbb{E}_{x}[||\phi(x)-\hat{\phi}(x)||^{2}] . Lower MSE indicates better reconstruction fidelity. This metric is widely used across SAE evaluation frameworks [ Bricken et al., 2023 , Cunningham et al., 2024 , Karvonen et al., 2025 ] and provides a stable, interpretable measure of how well the SAE preserves activation information.

sections.heading: Cross-Entropy Loss Recovery.
sections.text: Multiple early SAE works [ Bricken et al., 2023 , Cunningham et al., 2024 ] extended evaluation to measure whether SAEs preserve model performance when their reconstructions replace original activations, testing reconstruction fidelity via downstream loss. Cross-entropy loss recovery measures the cross-entropy loss when SAE reconstructions are passed through the model’s downstream layers, comparing it to both the baseline loss (without SAE) and the ablation loss (when activations are set to zero). The derived ce_loss_score metric normalizes performance preservation: ce_loss_score = ( ce_loss_with_ablation − ce_loss_with_sae ) / ( ce_loss_with_ablation − ce_loss_without_sae ) \text{ce\_loss\_score}=(\text{ce\_loss\_with\_ablation}-\text{ce\_loss\_with\_sae})/(\text{ce\_loss\_with\_ablation}-\text{ce\_loss\_without\_sae}) . This metric captures how well the SAE maintains the model’s predictive capabilities, which is critical for using SAEs in attribution and intervention tasks.

sections.heading: KL Divergence.
sections.text: Kullback-Leibler divergence measures the divergence between the distribution of the model’s output predictions when using original activations versus SAE reconstructions. Similar to cross-entropy loss recovery, KL divergence assesses whether the SAE preserves the model’s behavior distribution, not just point estimates. The derived kl_div_score metric normalizes by comparing to ablation: kl_div_score = ( kl_div_with_ablation − kl_div_with_sae ) / kl_div_with_ablation \text{kl\_div\_score}=(\text{kl\_div\_with\_ablation}-\text{kl\_div\_with\_sae})/\text{kl\_div\_with\_ablation} . This metric is particularly important for ensuring that SAE reconstructions preserve the model’s uncertainty and distributional behavior [ Karvonen et al., 2025 ] . These three metrics are computed over validation batches, using the same activation layers as those used in training. MSE is directly computed from activation reconstructions, while cross-entropy and KL divergence require passing reconstructions through the model’s decoder and output layers. Our implementation follows standard SAE evaluation practices [ Karvonen et al., 2025 , Bloom et al., 2024 ] . In the main paper we report MSE alone for completeness, although cross-entropy loss recovery and KL divergence offer complementary perspectives. To check that this choice does not change relative SAE rankings, we additionally computed explained variance ( R 2 R^{2} ) and cosine similarity across the full benchmark and measured pairwise Spearman correlations against MSE. The agreement is near-perfect: r s = − 0.99 r_{s}=-0.99 to − 1.00 -1.00 for MSE vs. R 2 R^{2} , r s = − 0.97 r_{s}=-0.97 to − 0.99 -0.99 for MSE vs. cossim (all p < 10 − 30 p<10^{-30} ). Figure 6 shows the pairwise scatter. Figure 6 : Pairwise scatter of MSE against R 2 R^{2} (plotted as VIF = 1 / ( 1 − R 2 ) \text{VIF}=1/(1-R^{2}) for log-scale clarity) and cosine similarity, across 610 SAEs from 7 families. MSE ranks SAEs near-identically to both alternatives ( | r s | ≥ 0.97 |r_{s}|\geq 0.97 ), confirming MSE as a valid simplifying proxy for reporting.

sections.heading: D.3 Proxy Metrics for Monosemanticity (C3)
sections.text: For C3 (Monosemanticity) , we introduce the Dominance-Aware Monosemanticity Evaluation (DAME), a comprehensive evaluation framework that addresses critical limitations of existing automated interpretability scoring methods. DAME is detailed in Section 3.2 of the main paper; here we provide complete implementation details.

sections.heading: From the C3 criterion to checkable evidence.
sections.text: An explainer uses construction examples to propose an activation-conditioned account e i e_{i} , expressed at the chosen granularity of 𝒞 \mathcal{C} , of what unit u i u_{i} represents; e i e_{i} is a candidate account, not an assumed optimum. An evaluator (the judge, in DAME) then uses e i e_{i} to predict an activation-derived target y i ​ ( z ) y_{i}(z) on a held-out item z z , producing p e i ​ ( z ) p_{e_{i}}(z) , and a higher-is-better scoring rule s s compares this prediction with the observed target. Let p 0 ​ ( z ) p_{0}(z) denote the uninformative baseline prediction. The explanation-specific lift is P i ​ ( e i ) = 𝔼 z ​ [ s ⁡ ( p e i ​ ( z ) , y i ​ ( z ) ) ] − 𝔼 z ​ [ s ⁡ ( p 0 ​ ( z ) , y i ​ ( z ) ) ] , P_{i}(e_{i})=\mathbb{E}_{z}\bigl[s(p_{e_{i}}(z),y_{i}(z))\bigr]-\mathbb{E}_{z}\bigl[s(p_{0}(z),y_{i}(z))\bigr], where 𝔼 z \mathbb{E}_{z} averages over held-out validation items. Binary detection, magnitude prediction, and DAME instantiate different choices of z z , y i y_{i} , and s s ; DAME uses held-out low-, medium-, and high-activation ordering. Positive lift means that the proposed explanation predicts held-out feature behavior beyond the uninformative baseline. It tests the predictive adequacy of that account; because it neither enumerates all concepts in 𝒞 \mathcal{C} nor determines how many concepts map to u i u_{i} , it does not itself test injectivity. It is therefore checkable evidence relevant to C3, but neither a logical consequence nor a sufficient proof of C3.

sections.heading: D.3.1 DAME Overview
sections.text: DAME evaluates SAE feature interpretability using a dominance-aware approach with a 3-way ranking task. Features are ranked by mean dominance (average contribution percentage across all input tokens), not firing frequency. The evaluation uses a 3-bin strategy and asks the LLM to rank 3 examples by activation strength.

sections.heading: Feature Discovery and Dominance Calculation.
sections.text: DAME uses a two-pass activation collection strategy to enable efficient evaluation: Pass 0 (Fast Dominance Counting): We compute mean dominance for each feature across N N batches (typically 50 for discovery). For each batch: • Get tokens: batch_tokens = store.get_batch_tokens() → [ batch_size = 32 , seq_len = 16 ] \text{batch\_tokens}=\text{store.get\_batch\_tokens()}\to[\text{batch\_size}=32,\text{seq\_len}=16] • Get model activations: model_acts = store.get_activations ​ ( batch_tokens ) → [ batch , seq , d in ] \text{model\_acts}=\text{store.get\_activations}(\text{batch\_tokens})\to[\text{batch},\text{seq},d_{\text{in}}] • Encode through SAE: sae_acts = sae.encode ​ ( model_acts_flat ) → [ batch × seq , m ] \text{sae\_acts}=\text{sae.encode}(\text{model\_acts\_flat})\to[\text{batch}\times\text{seq},m] • For each token position and each feature, compute dominance: ρ i ​ ( x ) = | f i ​ ( ϕ ⁡ ( x ) ) | / ∑ j | f j ​ ( ϕ ⁡ ( x ) ) | \rho_{i}(x)=|f_{i}(\phi(x))|/\sum_{j}|f_{j}(\phi(x))| • Sum dominance across all token positions After all batches, we compute mean dominance: ρ ¯ i = 𝔼 x ​ [ ρ i ​ ( x ) ] = dominance_sum ​ [ i ] / total_token_positions \bar{\rho}_{i}=\mathbb{E}_{x}[\rho_{i}(x)]=\text{dominance\_sum}[i]/\text{total\_token\_positions} . We also count firing sequences (for filtering): firing_count ​ [ i ] = count of sequences where max_activation > 0 \text{firing\_count}[i]=\text{count of sequences where max\_activation}>0 . This pass requires only O ⁡ ( m ) O(m) memory (storing dominance sums and counts, not activations) and completes in approximately 2–3 minutes for typical SAE sizes.

sections.heading: Feature Filtering and Quantile Sampling.
sections.text: We filter features to keep only those with ≥ 80 \geq 80 sequence firings (ensuring enough data for the 3-bin strategy: 20 for explanation + 40 for evaluation split into bin_A and bin_B + 20 for bin_C = 80 total). We then sort filtered features by mean dominance (descending)—not firing frequency—and split into 4 quantiles (Q1: 0–25%, Q2: 25–50%, Q3: 50–75%, Q4: 75–100%). We sample 20 features from each quantile = 80 total features per SAE. Dominance-based ranking captures each feature’s average contribution percentage, which is more theoretically sound than firing frequency and ensures fair evaluation across the dominance spectrum.

sections.heading: Collection and 3-Bin Strategy.
sections.text: We collect all sequences for sampled features by scanning the same batches as Pass 0. For each batch and each sampled feature: • Get all sequences where the feature activated • Compute max_activation (for token-based) and sum_activation (for sentence-based) • Store all sequences (not just top N N ) After all batches, for each feature: • Sort all sequences by activation magnitude (descending) • Reserve top 20 sequences for explanation generation (excluded from evaluation) • For remaining sequences: split at 50% mark → \to HIGH half (top 50% of remaining) and LOW half (bottom 50% of remaining) • Split HIGH half in the middle → \to BIN A (top 20) and BIN B (next 20) • LOW half → \to BIN C (bottom 20, may include non-firing sequences) The 3-bin result: • Top 20 sequences → \to Reserved for explanation (excluded from questions) • BIN A (HIGH-high): Next 20 sequences with highest activations (top half of evaluation sequences after removing explanation set) • BIN B (HIGH-low): Next 20 sequences with lower activations (bottom half of HIGH evaluation sequences) • BIN C (LOW): Bottom 20 sequences (lowest activations, may include non-firing) Critically, bin_A has higher activations than bin_B (ensured by sorting before splitting). We maintain separate bins for token-based evaluation (sorted by max_activation ) and sentence-based evaluation (sorted by sum_activation ).

sections.heading: Explanation Generation.
sections.text: For each sampled feature, we generate explanations using the top 20 sequences (excluded from evaluation). We build a prompt showing each sequence with: (1) the full sentence (all tokens concatenated), and (2) the top activation token (the single token with highest activation in that sequence). We do not show raw activation values to the LLM, ensuring fairness across features. We call the LLM ( Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 , run locally) to generate an explanation. Constraints (V2): • 40 token limit: max_new_tokens = 40 \text{max\_new\_tokens}=40 • 15 word maximum: System prompt explicitly states “Explain in ONE complete sentence, maximum 15 words.” • No frequency mentions: Cannot mention “often”, “frequently”, “rarely”, etc. • Focus on content: What lexical/syntactic/semantic patterns cause activation We track which sequences were used for explanation (to exclude from evaluation), preventing data leakage.

sections.heading: 3-Way Ranking Evaluation.
sections.text: We test whether explanations can correctly rank examples by activation strength using a 3-way ranking task: Token-Based Evaluation: For each feature, we sample 1 sequence from each bin (A, B, C) for each of 20 questions. We pick the highest-activating token from each sequence and build a ranking question: Given the explanation: [EXPLANATION] Rank these 3 examples by activation strength (1=highest, 2=middle, 3=lowest): Example A: [text with highlighted token] Example B: [text with highlighted token] Example C: [text with highlighted token] Output only: A=?, B=?, C=? The prompt does not show activation values. We call the same LLM to rank the examples. The true ranking is A=1 (highest), B=2 (middle), C=3 (lowest), reflecting that bin_A has higher activations than bin_B. Sentence-Based Evaluation: Similar to token-based, but we use bin_A_sum_sequences , bin_B_sum_sequences , bin_C_sum_sequences and ask the LLM to rank entire sentences by activation strength.

sections.heading: Scoring (4 Metrics per Question).
sections.text: For each ranking question, we compute 4 metrics: 1. Perfect ranking accuracy: Did the LLM get the exact order correct? (A=1, B=2, C=3) 2. Rank correlation: Spearman correlation between predicted and true ranking 3. Pairwise accuracy: A vs B, B vs C, A vs C—fraction of pairwise comparisons correct 4. Rank distance: Average absolute difference in rank positions We aggregate these metrics per feature (mean across questions) and then per-quantile (mean across features in each quantile).

sections.heading: Memory Management.
sections.text: The two-pass strategy enables memory-efficient evaluation: • Pass 0: O ⁡ ( m ) O(m) memory—only stores dominance sums and counts • Collection: O ⁡ ( 80 × sequences_per_feature ) O(80\times\text{sequences\_per\_feature}) memory—stores sequences only for selected features (not all features) • Binning: In-place sorting and splitting After each SAE evaluation, we delete all sequence storage, clear GPU cache, and garbage collect, enabling evaluation of many SAEs in sequence without memory issues.

sections.heading: D.3.2 Synthetic Validation of DAME on Ground-Truth Concepts
sections.text: DAME relies on an LLM-as-judge proxy for monosemanticity. To verify that the dominance–monosemanticity relationship reflects a genuine property of SAE decompositions rather than a measurement artifact, we replicate the Section 4.1 analysis on a synthetic benchmark with known ground-truth concepts.

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: We generate synthetic activations from 128 ground-truth concepts and train 105 SAEs spanning all 7 architectures (Standard, TopK, BatchTopK, Matryoshka, JumpReLU, Gated, PAnneal), 3 widths, and 5 sparsity levels (15 SAEs per architecture).

sections.heading: Ground-truth monosemanticity gap.
sections.text: For each feature i i , we compute its activation correlation with each ground-truth concept c k c_{k} and report the gap between the best and second-best concept correlation; a large gap indicates the feature is monosemantically aligned with a single ground-truth concept. We then test, per SAE, whether Q1 (top-quartile dominance) features have a smaller gap than Q2–Q4 (one-sided Mann–Whitney U test, α = 0.05 \alpha=0.05 ).

sections.heading: Headline.
sections.text: 71 of 105 SAEs (68%) show a statistically significant Q1 deficit ( p < 0.05 p<0.05 ). The synthetic findings replicate the real-data pattern using ground truth instead of LLM judgment, consistent with the dominance–monosemanticity relationship.

sections.heading: Per-architecture pattern.
sections.text: JumpReLU shows the strongest Q1 deficit on the synthetic benchmark ( 15 / 15 SAEs significant); Gated is weakest ( 3 / 15 ) (Figure 7 ). This is the inverse of the real-data result, where JumpReLU was n.s. on SAEBench. The discrepancy is explained by hyperparameter mismatch: SAEBench-default JumpReLU has median L 0 = 691 L_{0}=691 , far above the saturation point at which dominance dilutes. With sparsity matched in synthetic training, JumpReLU’s architectural tendency toward dominant features re-emerges. This further supports the interpretation in Section 4.1 : the real-data n.s. result for JumpReLU/Gated reflects hyperparameter choice, not architectural exemption from the Q1 deficit. Figure 7 : Synthetic validation of DAME on ground-truth concepts. For each architecture, horizontal bars show the Q1 monosemanticity deficit (mean Q1 − - mean Q2–Q4) of each individual SAE; stars mark statistical significance (Mann–Whitney U, p < 0.05 p<0.05 ). Subplot titles show the per-architecture count of significant SAEs out of 15: JumpReLU 15/15 (strongest); Gated 3/15 (weakest). 71 of 105 SAEs (68%) overall show significant Q1 deficit.

sections.heading: Dead Features.
sections.text: Dead features—those not activating meaningfully across training or evaluation data—present a persistent challenge in SAE training and evaluation. Without appropriate mitigations, a large fraction of SAE features can become dead, wasting dictionary capacity and reducing the effective number of learned features. Templeton et al. [2024] reported that their 34M latent SAE had only 12M alive latents (approximately 65% dead); without mitigations, up to 90% of features can die during training. This problem is particularly acute in architectures with explicit sparsity constraints (e.g., TopK), where features may be initialized in regions of activation space that rarely activate. Multiple solutions have been proposed to address dead features: • Encoder-decoder initialization: Initializing the encoder as the transpose of the decoder provides an initial alignment that encourages feature utilization [ Templeton et al., 2024 ] . • Auxiliary losses: Providing gradient signal to dead features through auxiliary reconstruction losses ensures they receive updates even when rarely activating [ Gao et al., 2025 ] . • Ghost gradients: Anthropic’s “ghost grads” technique artificially injects gradients for dead features, simulating activation patterns to keep them alive during training [ Templeton et al., 2024 ] . These techniques have proven effective: Templeton et al. [2024] report that OpenAI’s 16M latent GPT-4 SAE achieved only 7% dead latents through a combination of these approaches.

sections.heading: Metrics.
sections.text: We evaluate dead feature rates by counting features that have zero (or near-zero, below threshold) activations across evaluation batches. We report both the proportion of dead features (features with firing frequency below threshold, typically 10 − 4 10^{-4} activation threshold) and firing frequency statistics (mean, median, quartiles of feature firing frequencies). These metrics help identify poor usage of dictionary capacity and indicate whether SAE training succeeded in utilizing the full feature set.

sections.heading: D.5 Proxy Metrics for Per-Input Sparsity (C5)
sections.text: For C5 (Per-input sparsity) , we evaluate how sparse SAE activations are, both for individual inputs and across datasets. High per-input activation counts can make an attribution difficult to inspect even when individual features are monosemantic.

sections.heading: Average Active Features.
sections.text: The standard sparsity metric counts how many features activate per input, where a feature is considered “active” if its absolute activation value exceeds a threshold (typically 10 − 5 10^{-5} ). We compute the average number of active features across all inputs: avg_active_features = 𝔼 x [ ∑ i 𝟏 [ | f i ( ϕ ( x ) ) | > τ ] ] \text{avg\_active\_features}=\mathbb{E}_{x}[\sum_{i}\mathbf{1}[|f_{i}(\phi(x))|>\tau]] . This matches the common intuition in prior work that sparsity refers to how many features fire for one input sequence.

sections.heading: Effective Sparsity.
sections.text: However, simple counting can be misleading for architectures where negligible activations are not explicitly penalized (e.g., TopK-like architectures, where many features may have tiny but non-zero activations). To make sparsity metrics more accurate, we also report 75% and 95% effective sparsity : for each input, we count how many features (when sorted by absolute activation) are needed to sum up to the specified percentile (75% or 95%) of total absolute activation. Formally, for input x x , let sorted_acts = sort ​ ( | f i ​ ( ϕ ⁡ ( x ) ) | ) \text{sorted\_acts}=\text{sort}(|f_{i}(\phi(x))|) (descending). We compute: effective_active p ​ ( x ) = min ⁡ { k : ∑ i = 1 k sorted_acts ​ [ i ] ∑ j sorted_acts ​ [ j ] ≥ p / 100 } \text{effective\_active}_{p}(x)=\min\left\{k:\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\text{sorted\_acts}[i]}{\sum_{j}\text{sorted\_acts}[j]}\geq p/100\right\} and report 𝔼 x ​ [ effective_active p ​ ( x ) ] \mathbb{E}_{x}[\text{effective\_active}_{p}(x)] for p ∈ { 75 , 95 } p\in\{75,95\} . This captures tail behavior: many features may be negligible though not strictly zero, and effective sparsity measures the number of features that actually contribute to the reconstruction.

sections.heading: Data-Wise vs Feature-Wise Sparsity.
sections.text: We distinguish between two perspectives on sparsity that are sometimes conflated: Data-wise sparsity (what most people intuitively mean): For a given input sequence, how many features fire? This is the standard per-input L 0 L_{0} norm and matches common intuition. Feature-wise sparsity (what loss functions often implicitly optimize): Across the dataset, on how many inputs does a feature fire? When designing loss functions, researchers control or minimize the overall activation amount, which also minimizes the number of inputs on which each feature fires. This matches more closely with monosemanticity—when a feature fires less often, it may in some cases imply better monosemanticity (unless there is a feature-split problem) or at least better interpretability. In both other papers and in our work, sparsity is fundamentally and practically talking about the number of features fired for one input (data-wise sparsity). However, as sparsity highly correlates with monosemanticity both in results and in loss design, this can be confusing sometimes and cause potential problems in people’s theoretical work. We report both data-wise metrics (average active features per input) and feature-wise statistics (firing frequency distributions) to provide a complete picture. Our implementation computes these metrics across evaluation batches, processing activations in chunks to avoid memory issues for large SAEs. For effective sparsity calculations, we process inputs sequentially, computing cumulative activation sums and identifying the minimum number of features needed to reach each percentile threshold.

sections.heading: D.6 Empirical Mapping to SAEBench Evaluations
sections.text: The five AIU criteria can be empirically validated against existing SAEBench evaluations [ Karvonen et al., 2025 ] . Each SAEBench evaluation tests downstream task performance under specific failure modes; we map each evaluation to the AIU criteria it implicitly probes (treating evaluations that depend on multiple criteria as joint proxies rather than direct proxies for a single criterion). We then verify each mapping empirically across 246 SAEs (SAEBench Gemma + SAEBench Pythia, 3 widths ∈ { 4 ​ k , 16 ​ k , 65 ​ k } \in\{4\text{k},16\text{k},65\text{k}\} ; RAVEL and Unlearning are Gemma-only because Pythia lacks an instruct variant and is too small for reliable attribute prediction). We use SAEBench’s ce_loss_score as the C2 proxy, SAEBench’s autointerp score as the C3 proxy, and our dead-feature-filtered redundancy score as the C1 proxy.

sections.heading: Joint-proxy methodology.
sections.text: For each proposed criterion pair (e.g., C2+C3), we (i) rank SAEs on each criterion within each (model, width) group to control for scale confounds, (ii) take the product of the two within-group ranks as a joint proxy that is high only when both criteria are high, and (iii) compute Spearman correlation between this product and the SAEBench evaluation score across the pooled 246 SAEs. Trains a k k -sparse linear probe on the top-5 SAE features per class. C2 ensures the task-relevant signal is captured at all; C3 ensures each of those 5 features carries clean single-concept information so the probe can succeed with so few features. • SCR (Spurious Correlation Removal) → \rightarrow C2 + + C3, r s = + 0.459 ∗ ∗ ∗ r_{s}=+0.459^{***} . Ablates SAE features correlated with a spurious attribute and measures recovery toward clean behavior. C2 ensures the spurious signal is captured (and thus removable); C3 ensures the ablation is surgical—removing the spurious signal without collateral damage to the true task signal. • Feature Absorption → \rightarrow C1 + + C3, r s = + 0.248 ∗ ∗ ∗ r_{s}=+0.248^{***} . Tests whether broad features absorb the signal of more specific ones (e.g., a generic “Paris” feature absorbing first-letter knowledge). Absorption is a form of feature entanglement — the opposite of C1; C3 ensures each feature captures one concept cleanly and so absorbs less.

sections.heading: Conceptually C1 + + C3, empirically C2-bottlenecked (2/8).
sections.text: TPP (Targeted Probe Perturbation) ablates the top SAE features for a target class and measures whether the target class drops more than other classes. RAVEL learns a binary mask over SAE features to isolate one attribute of an entity, swaps masked features between entities, and decodes through the SAE to check whether the model’s output changes accordingly. Both were proposed as C1 + + C3 evaluations: C1 because non-redundant features have no backup copies that can compensate for ablation, and C3 because monosemantic features make the perturbation precise. Empirically, however, both are dominated by C2 (TPP: r s , C2 = + 0.768 ∗ ∗ ∗ r_{s,\mathrm{C2}}=+0.768^{***} ; RAVEL: r s , C2 = + 0.971 ∗ ∗ ∗ r_{s,\mathrm{C2}}=+0.971^{***} ): the encode-modify-decode pipeline requires the SAE to first capture a concept faithfully before any C1/C3 intervention can be tested. If the SAE cannot reconstruct the activations that encode the target attribute, ablation or swapping cannot have the intended effect regardless of feature distinctness or interpretability.
