sections.text: Unlearning ablates the top SAE features and reports the largest drop in dangerous-knowledge accuracy (WMDP-bio) achievable while preserving general capabilities (MMLU ≥ 0.99 \geq 0.99 ). All three of C1, C2, C3 should matter in principle: C1 because redundant copies of dangerous-knowledge features survive ablation of any one copy; C2 because the dangerous concept must be captured to be ablated; C3 because monosemantic features cleanly separate dangerous from safe content. Empirically, however, r s , C3 = + 0.494 ∗ ∗ ∗ r_{s,\mathrm{C3}}=+0.494^{***} dominates, r s , C2 = − 0.562 ∗ ∗ ∗ r_{s,\mathrm{C2}}=-0.562^{***} (negative), and r s , C1 r_{s,\mathrm{C1}} is not significant. The likely reason: unlearning targets one specific concept (bioweapons knowledge), not an aggregate, so global C1 and C2 proxies—which average across many concepts—may not vary enough to predict whether this particular concept was captured. The negative C2 correlation is most plausibly inherited from the C2 ↔ \leftrightarrow C3 anti-correlation rather than causal.

sections.heading: C2 ↔ \leftrightarrow C3 anti-correlation as a diagnostic feature.
sections.text: At small SAE widths the SAEBench analysis reveals a strong negative pooled correlation between completeness (C2) and monosemanticity (C3): r s = − 0.66 r_{s}=-0.66 overall, − 0.88 -0.88 at width 4k. This is precisely why TPP and RAVEL—both nominally C1 + + C3 evaluations—are bottlenecked by C2 in practice: at small widths an SAE must trade reconstruction fidelity for per-feature interpretability. The framework thus predicts , rather than merely describes, this downstream failure mode.

sections.heading: Appendix E Automated Interpretability Scoring: Prior Work
sections.text: The landscape of automated interpretability scoring has evolved rapidly since OpenAI’s foundational work, with two systems establishing the dominant paradigms: Bills et al.’s simulation-based approach [ Bills et al., 2023 ] and EleutherAI’s Delphi detection-based system [ Paulo et al., 2024 ] . This appendix provides detailed implementation specifications for these systems and documents how major SAE papers deploy them in practice.

sections.heading: E.1 Overview of Automated Interpretability Scoring
sections.text: Automated interpretability scoring aims to quantify whether individual features in neural networks respond to coherent, singular concepts—directly operationalizing the monosemanticity objective that motivated SAE development. These systems generally follow a three-stage pipeline: (1) explanation generation, where a language model produces natural language descriptions from feature activation patterns; (2) scoring, where the quality of explanations is evaluated through prediction tasks; and (3) aggregation, where feature-level scores combine into global metrics. Two systems dominate current practice. OpenAI’s approach [ Bills et al., 2023 ] introduced simulation-based scoring using GPT-4, establishing the paradigm that subsequent work built upon. EleutherAI’s Delphi system [ Paulo et al., 2024 ] fundamentally redesigned the scoring methodology to achieve approximately 150× cost reduction through detection scoring and open-source models, making large-scale evaluation tractable. We detail each system’s methodology before examining how major SAE papers adapt these approaches.

sections.heading: E.2 Bills et al. (2023): Simulation-Based Scoring with GPT-4
sections.text: OpenAI’s “Language Models Can Explain Neurons in Language Models” [ Bills et al., 2023 ] introduced the dominant automated interpretability framework through a three-step process: explanation generation, simulation, and correlation scoring. The system analyzed all 307,200 neurons in GPT-2 XL, though only approximately 1,000 (0.33%) achieved explanation scores ≥ 0.8 \geq 0.8 .

sections.heading: Explanation Generation.
sections.text: The system uses GPT-4 to generate natural language descriptions from 5 top-activating text excerpts, each containing 64 contiguous tokens sampled from the pre-training distribution. Raw neuron activations undergo preprocessing: negative values are clamped to zero, remaining positive values are linearly scaled to a 0–10 range, then discretized to integers. For sparse neurons (activating on < 20 % <20\% of tokens), the system uses modified prompts that include only non-zero token-activation pairs, helping the model focus on relevant activation patterns rather than long sequences of zeros.

sections.heading: Simulation Scoring.
sections.text: The core innovation is “simulation” scoring: GPT-4, given only the generated explanation, predicts how the neuron would activate on new sequences. The simulator outputs integer predictions from 0–10 for each token. The Pearson correlation coefficient between simulated and actual activations serves as the primary metric: Score = corr ​ ( predicted activations , actual activations ) . \text{Score}=\text{corr}(\text{predicted activations},\text{actual activations}). Two evaluation modes exist: “random-only” using 5 uniformly random excerpts, and “top-and-random” using a mix of 5 top-activating plus 5 random excerpts—the latter providing variance reduction at the cost of some bias toward high-activation patterns.

sections.heading: Validation and Limitations.
sections.text: The paper validated simulation scoring against an expensive “ablation scoring” gold standard, computed as: 1 − 𝔼 x [ AvgJSD ( m ( x , n = s ( x ) ) ∥ m ( x ) ) ] 𝔼 x [ AvgJSD ( m ( x , n = μ ) ∥ m ( x ) ) ] , 1-\frac{\mathbb{E}_{x}[\text{AvgJSD}(m(x,n=s(x))\parallel m(x))]}{\mathbb{E}_{x}[\text{AvgJSD}(m(x,n=\mu)\parallel m(x))]}, where m ⁡ ( x , n = v ) m(x,n=v) denotes the model’s output distribution when neuron n n is set to value v v , demonstrating that correlation scoring serves as a reasonable proxy for causal importance. Critical limitations acknowledged include: (1) explanations are correlative rather than mechanistic, (2) scores degrade significantly with larger subject models, and (3) many neurons exhibit polysemanticity—activating on “five or six different things with no discernible pattern.” OpenAI released code at https://github.com/openai/automated-interpretability and public datasets on Azure blob storage, including per-neuron activations and explanations with simulation results.

sections.heading: E.3 EleutherAI Delphi (2024): Detection Scoring at Scale
sections.text: EleutherAI’s Delphi system [ Paulo et al., 2024 ] fundamentally redesigns the scoring methodology to achieve approximately $1,300 for 1.5M features versus approximately $200,000 for prior methods using closed-source models. The key insight: detection and fuzzing scoring require far fewer tokens and enable use of open-source models like Llama 3.1 70B Instruct quantized with AWQ to INT4.

sections.heading: Detection and Fuzzing Scoring.
sections.text: The critical innovation moves from token-level simulation to sequence-level detection. Rather than asking an LLM to predict activation values for every token, detection scoring asks whether whole sequences contain a feature—a simpler classification task. Detection uses activating examples sampled from quantiles of the activation distribution plus random non-activating examples, measuring both precision and recall rather than just recall. Fuzzing scoring marks tokens with << and >> delimiters and asks the model to identify which examples are correctly marked, using 7 activating examples from each of 10 quantiles (5 correctly marked, 2 incorrectly marked) for 70 total examples. This approach directly tests whether explanations capture the specific token-level patterns that trigger activation. Method Prompt Tokens Output Tokens Runtime (5 ex.) Explanation 397 + 566 29.90 3.14s Detection/Fuzzing 725 + 53 11.99 4.29s Simulation 24,074.85 1,598.1 73.9s Table 4: Token and runtime comparison between scoring methods. Detection and fuzzing achieve comparable accuracy with approximately 5× fewer tokens and 17× less runtime than simulation.

sections.heading: Quantile-Based Sampling.
sections.text: Delphi’s sampling strategy marks another departure from Bills et al. The team found that sampling only top-N examples produces narrow explanations that fail to capture behavior across the full distribution, while uniform sampling produces overly broad explanations. The solution: sample evenly from all activation quantiles to match train/test distributions, achieving higher scores. The system uses << and >> delimiter syntax to highlight max-activating tokens in context rather than listing tokens with tabs. Detection + fuzzing balanced accuracy shows Pearson correlation of 0.61 with traditional simulation scoring while costing approximately 5× fewer tokens and 17× less runtime. The EleutherAI pipeline filters problematic features before expensive explanation: positional features (identified via mutual information with position > 0.05 >0.05 ) and unigram features ( ≤ 20 \leq 20 unique tokens in top 80% activations) are flagged and handled separately.

sections.heading: E.4 Adoption in Major SAE Papers
sections.text: Each major SAE publication adapts automated interpretability differently, revealing an evolution in methodology and growing recognition of limitations.

sections.heading: Bricken et al. (2023): Direct Application of Bills et al.
sections.text: “Towards Monosemanticity” [ Bricken et al., 2023 ] directly applies Bills et al. methodology using GPT-4 as both explainer and simulator. The paper evaluated all 4,096 features in their A/1 SAE, computing both activation-based and logit-weight-based auto-interpretability scores. They used top activating examples plus random samples from quantiles, finding that most learned features are interpretable. The paper acknowledged that interpretations may not capture all aspects of features’ behaviors.

sections.heading: Templeton et al. (2024): Rubric-Based Scoring.
sections.text: “Scaling Monosemanticity” [ Templeton et al., 2024 ] developed a custom rubric-based system using Claude 3 for both explanation generation and scoring. Rather than correlation scores, features receive relevance ratings: “highly relevant,” “somewhat relevant,” or “not relevant.” This simplification was necessary for scale—the paper examined SAEs with 1M, 4M, and 34M latents where evaluating all features is computationally intractable. Random sampling with top-activating examples found SAE features substantially more interpretable than neurons (25% of neurons are highly relevant). The paper noted that later layers are harder to interpret and many features exhibit “cross-layer superposition.”

sections.heading: Cunningham et al. (2024): Automated Interpretability with Layer Analysis.
sections.text: Cunningham et al. [ Cunningham et al., 2024 ] represents the first major SAE paper systematically applying Bills et al. automated interpretability, demonstrating that SAE features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA directions, or random directions. They sampled random nonzero activations (up to 16) to build explanations with another 16 as true positives for recall. Key finding: interpretability scores decrease in later layers, suggesting features may be more complex or require examining output effects rather than just input patterns.

sections.heading: Gao et al. (2024): Critique of Recall Bias.
sections.text: “Scaling and Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders” [ Gao et al., 2025 ] from OpenAI introduced significant methodological innovations while explicitly critiquing recall bias in Bills et al. scoring. They adopted Neuron2Graph (N2G), which generates collections of n-grams with wildcards rather than natural language—cheaper but less expressive. Crucially, they separated precision and recall metrics: explanation precision measures how many tokens matching explanations actually activate features, while recall measures how many activations are explained. Their key critique: Bills et al. scoring disproportionately depends on recall, meaning broad explanations score well even when inaccurate. Example: a “stop” explanation scores highly when the actual feature is “don’t stop” or “can’t stop”—a problem that becomes more severe as features get sparser and more specific.

sections.heading: Karvonen et al. (2025): SAEBench Synthesis.
sections.text: SAEBench [ Karvonen et al., 2025 ] synthesizes prior work into a comprehensive benchmark with 8 diverse metrics. For automated interpretability specifically, they use gpt-4o-mini as an LLM judge with detection scoring similar to EleutherAI’s Delphi system [ Paulo et al., 2024 ] . The generation phase collects SAE activations on webtext, selects top-k sequences plus importance-weighted samples, formats with <<token>> highlighting, and prompts for explanations. The scoring phase creates test sets mixing top activation sequences, importance-weighted sequences, and random sequences. A crucial finding: automated interpretability struggles to provide statistically significant differences between SAE architectures, with Anthropic team members noting “most SAE variants perform comparably” on autointerp. This suggests that automated interpretability scores alone may be insufficient for SAE evaluation.

sections.heading: E.5 Other Technical Implementation Details
sections.text: The technical details of these systems involve numerous design choices that significantly affect results.

sections.heading: Activation Thresholding.
sections.text: Activation thresholding varies by architecture. TopK SAEs directly enforce sparsity by keeping only k k largest latents (typical k ∈ { 32 , 64 , 128 } k\in\{32,64,128\} ), eliminating need for L 1 L_{1} penalties and preventing activation shrinkage. JumpReLU applies learned threshold θ \theta with formula J θ ​ ( x ) = x ⋅ 𝟙 ( x > θ ) J_{\theta}(x)=x\cdot\mathbb{1}_{(x>\theta)} , requiring approximate gradients. Standard ReLU uses implicit threshold at zero with sparsity controlled by L 1 L_{1} coefficient λ \lambda (typical values: α ≈ 7.7 × 10 − 2 \alpha\approx 7.7\times 10^{-2} ). Gated SAEs separate selection of which latents are active from estimation of magnitudes.

sections.heading: Feature Sampling for Evaluation.
sections.text: Sampling strategies operate at two levels. Within-feature sampling determines which examples to show when generating explanations: EleutherAI samples from 10 activation deciles of each feature’s distribution, ensuring explanations capture both weak and strong activations; N2G uses up to 16 random nonzero activations. Between-feature sampling determines which features to evaluate: SAEBench samples 1,000 non-dead latents using probe attribution; standard approaches use uniform random sampling of features, which may underrepresent dominant features that contribute most to model behavior.

sections.heading: Aggregation Methods.
sections.text: Aggregation methods typically employ mean or median. SAEBench reports “median score and interquartile (25%–75%) range.” EleutherAI uses mean with error bars. OpenAI’s sparsity-of-effects metric uses ( L 1 / L 2 ) 2 (L_{1}/L_{2})^{2} ratio for downstream logit effects—SAE latents achieve 10–14% versus residual stream channels at approximately 60%. Self-similarity thresholds require separate optimization for different layer SAEs, with scores higher than approximately 0.01 generally indicating successful explanation generation.

sections.heading: E.6 Comparison to DAME (Our Approach)
sections.text: DAME (Dominance-Aware Monosemanticity Evaluation) addresses fundamental limitations in prior automated interpretability scoring through innovations at three stages: feature sampling, explanation generation, and aggregation. Activation-balanced contrastive validation Aggregation Uniform mean: 1 N ​ ∑ i s i \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}s_{i} Per-quantile + dominance-weighted: ∑ i w i dom ​ s i \sum_{i}w_{i}^{\text{dom}}s_{i} Table 5: Comparison of DAME to prior automated interpretability approaches.

sections.heading: Feature Sampling: From Uniform to Dominance-Stratified.
sections.text: Prior automated interpretability systems sample features uniformly at random [ Bills et al., 2023 , Bricken et al., 2023 , Cunningham et al., 2024 ] or based on probe attribution—correlation with downstream task performance [ Karvonen et al., 2025 ] . Both approaches face fundamental issues when features exhibit vastly different computational influence: Uniform sampling treats all features equally, regardless of their contribution to model behavior. In a typical SAE with power-law dominance distribution, a uniform sample of 100 features might include 1–2 features from the top dominance quartile (which collectively account for > 50 % >50\% of reconstruction magnitude) and 50+ features from the bottom quartile (contributing < 5 % <5\% ). When these per-feature scores are averaged with equal weight, the resulting global metric primarily reflects the monosemanticity of computationally negligible features. Probe-based sampling (SAEBench) selects features correlated with specific downstream tasks, but this measures task-relevant feature quality rather than the overall feature dictionary quality. A feature dictionary could excel on pre-selected supervised tasks while failing catastrophically on the dominant features that drive most model computation. DAME introduces dominance-stratified feature sampling : features are ranked by mean dominance ρ ¯ i \bar{\rho}_{i} and divided into dominance quantiles, sampling equal numbers from each quantile. This ensures evaluation coverage across the full dominance spectrum, from dominant features contributing > 1 % >1\% of average reconstruction to rare features contributing < 0.001 % <0.001\% .

sections.heading: Explanation Generation: Ensuring Comparable Information.
sections.text: Prior work directly shows activation magnitudes during explanation generation [ Bills et al., 2023 , Templeton et al., 2024 , Paulo et al., 2024 ] , creating systematic bias: features with different firing frequencies and magnitude distributions receive qualitatively different information: • High-frequency features activate on many tokens, providing numerous examples with varied contexts during explanation generation—high-entropy information that enables nuanced descriptions. • Rare features activate sparsely, providing few examples with limited context—low-entropy information that forces vague or overly specific descriptions. • Heavy-tailed features (common among dominant features) show extreme magnitude variation: displaying “activation = 0.0001” versus “activation = 10.0” signals very different feature importance, biasing explanation quality. Additionally, Bills et al. and subsequent work allow unbounded explanation length , enabling polysemantic features (especially dominant polysemantic features with diverse activation patterns) to list multiple unrelated triggers in a single description, artificially inflating scores. DAME addresses both issues: (1) activation magnitudes are hidden during explanation generation—the LLM sees only “this token triggered the feature” without magnitude information, ensuring comparable information across features with different magnitude distributions; (2) explanations are length-constrained , encouraging descriptions to identify a single coherent concept rather than enumerating multiple unrelated patterns.

sections.heading: Scoring: From Binary Classification to Ranked Bins.
sections.text: Existing scoring methodologies suffer from base rate problems when comparing features with different firing frequencies: Bills et al. simulation scoring computes Pearson correlation between predicted and actual activation values, but this is sensitive to the distribution of activations in the test set. For always-on features (activating on > 90 % >90\% of tokens), even random predictions achieve high correlation by chance. For rare features (activating on < 1 % <1\% of tokens), correlation is dominated by the abundant negative examples. Delphi detection scoring [ Paulo et al., 2024 ] frames scoring as binary classification: does the feature activate on this sequence or not? This improves upon simulation by measuring precision and recall explicitly, but the F1 score remains sensitive to base rate: a feature activating on 50% of tokens has balanced classes, while a feature activating on 1% has severe class imbalance (99:1 negative:positive ratio), making F1 scores incomparable across features. DAME introduces activation-balanced contrastive validation : for each feature, all test inputs are divided into three groups (low, medium, high activation) based on that feature’s own activation distribution using quantile splits, and the LLM ranks one example from each group by predicted activation strength. This design ensures: • Balanced comparison: All features receive exactly one example from each activation level, eliminating base rate effects. • Magnitude sensitivity: Unlike binary thresholding, ranking requires distinguishing strong from weak activations, directly testing whether explanations capture the full activation distribution rather than just presence/absence. • Comparable difficulty: The 3-way ranking task has identical structure for all features, making scores directly comparable across features with wildly different activation patterns. Ranking quality is measured through four complementary metrics (perfect ranking accuracy, rank correlation, pairwise accuracy, rank distance) that together provide robust assessment of explanation quality.

sections.heading: Aggregation: From Uniform Averaging to Dominance Weighting.
sections.text: Prior work aggregates feature-level scores through uniform averaging [ Bills et al., 2023 , Paulo et al., 2024 , Karvonen et al., 2025 ] : Global Score prior = 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N s i , \text{Global Score}_{\text{prior}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}s_{i}, treating all features as equally important regardless of their computational contribution. When combined with uniform feature sampling, this produces global metrics dominated by rare, low-influence features. DAME provides two complementary aggregation approaches: Per-quantile reporting separately reports monosemanticity for each dominance quantile: MonoScore Q q = 1 | Q q | ​ ∑ i ∈ Q q s i \text{MonoScore}^{Q_{q}}=\frac{1}{|Q_{q}|}\sum_{i\in Q_{q}}s_{i} for quantiles Q 1 , Q 2 , … , Q Q Q_{1},Q_{2},\ldots,Q_{Q} . This reveals whether dominant features are less monosemantic than rare features—a critical diagnostic for identifying failures where they matter most for model behavior. If MonoScore Q 1 ≪ MonoScore Q 4 \text{MonoScore}^{Q_{1}}\ll\text{MonoScore}^{Q_{4}} (highest-dominance quartile much worse than lowest), the SAE exhibits functional polysemanticity in its most important features despite potentially high average scores. Dominance-weighted aggregation provides a single summary metric for cross-SAE comparison: MonoScore DAME = ∑ i ∈ sample w i dom ⋅ s i , w i dom = ρ ¯ i ∑ j ∈ sample ρ ¯ j , \text{MonoScore}_{\text{DAME}}=\sum_{i\in\text{sample}}w_{i}^{\text{dom}}\cdot s_{i},\quad w_{i}^{\text{dom}}=\frac{\bar{\rho}_{i}}{\sum_{j\in\text{sample}}\bar{\rho}_{j}}, where each feature’s score is weighted by its mean dominance ρ ¯ i \bar{\rho}_{i} . This ensures that failures in dominant features (which drive model behavior) penalize the global score more than failures in negligible features. Together, DAME provides the first automated interpretability framework explicitly designed to evaluate monosemanticity where it matters most—in the dominant features that drive model computation. The innovations described above address key limitations in prior work: scores become comparable across features with different base rates (via activation-balanced contrastive validation), unbounded explanations can no longer reward polysemanticity (via length constraints), and binary thresholds no longer ignore magnitude distributions (via ranking across activation levels).

sections.heading: E.7 Monosemanticity vs. Automated Interpretability: A Fundamental Disconnect
sections.text: The unbounded explanations length problem mentioned earlier reveals a deeper conceptual issue: automated interpretability metrics fundamentally measure something different from monosemanticity. As discussed in Section 3.2 , when explanations can be arbitrarily long, polysemantic features can list multiple unrelated triggers, inflating scores [ Bills et al., 2023 , Paulo et al., 2024 ] . This particularly affects frequent polysemantic features, which receive more information during explanation generation, allowing multiple concepts to be covered as they have more activated examples. This observation exposes a critical tension in the field: while SAE research explicitly aims to address superposition and find monosemantic features—features that encode a single coherent concept—the dominant evaluation metrics used throughout the literature do not actually measure how many concepts each feature encodes. Instead, automated interpretability asks: for all the concepts that a feature can cover, are those concepts interpretable or conveyable? As long as the concepts can be conveyed (even if there are many of them), the feature is considered interpretable. Under this definition, automated interpretability is fundamentally different from monosemanticity. A polysemantic feature encoding five unrelated concepts can achieve high interpretability scores if all five concepts can be listed in an explanation, while a truly monosemantic feature encoding a single concept receives the same score. The metric does not distinguish between these cases—it measures whether concepts are conveyable, not whether there is a single concept. This disconnect means that claims about achieving monosemanticity based solely on automated interpretability scores are technically unsupported. A feature dictionary could achieve high average interpretability scores while remaining highly polysemantic, as long as the multiple concepts encoded by each feature can be enumerated in explanations. The field’s core objective—finding features that encode single concepts—requires metrics that explicitly penalize multi-concept encoding, which standard automated interpretability approaches do not provide.

Dead Feature Proportion: Dead feature proportions (firing frequency < 10 − 3 <10^{-3} ) show substantial variation across families and configurations. sections.heading: Key Observations.
sections.text: Several patterns emerge from this analysis: 1. Architecture-specific strengths: TopK architecture consistently achieves the best sparsity (lowest active features), while Gated architecture shows the best reconstruction fidelity (lowest MSE) on average. This suggests a potential trade-off between activation efficiency and reconstruction accuracy. 2. Family-specific variation: MSE values vary substantially across families (ranging from 10 − 4 10^{-4} for OPT-125M to 10 2 10^{2} for SAEBench Gemma), indicating that the underlying model and activation distribution significantly influence reconstruction difficulty. This variation makes cross-family comparisons less meaningful than within-family rankings. 3. Feature utilization variation: Across the 610 SAEs spanning all 7 architectures and 6 families, computed on ∼ \sim 122k validation tokens, the strict “never fires” rate (firing count = 0 =0 ) is near-zero for every architecture. Under a less strict threshold (firing frequency < 10 − 3 <10^{-3} ), per-SAE median dead rates vary widely: from near-zero for Gated SAEs to roughly 0–80% across the other architectures (with BatchTopK and Matryoshka highest). The very-rare threshold ( < 10 − 4 <10^{-4} ) gives a similarly wide spread. This variation underscores that “dead” is threshold-dependent and that achieving efficient feature utilization requires careful hyperparameter tuning, especially for sparse-activation architectures. 4. Hyperparameter sensitivity: The wide distributions within each architecture-family combination (visible in the box plots) indicate that hyperparameter settings play a crucial role in determining performance. This reinforces the importance of within-family comparisons rather than cross-family rankings.

sections.heading: Sample-size note for the redundancy dead-feature filter.
sections.text: The dead-feature filter applied in Section 4.2 uses a different sample. Specifically, dead features are detected as features with zero observed firings within the redundancy evaluation sample ( ∼ \sim 12k tokens, 3 batches × \times 4096 tokens). At this smaller sample size, a feature whose true firing frequency is ∼ \sim 10 − 5 10^{-5} has expected count ∼ \sim 0.12 and is often labelled as “dead.” In practice this approximates a “firing frequency < 10 − 4 <10^{-4} ” threshold rather than a strict “never fires” threshold. The dead-feature rates reported above (122k tokens) and the per-architecture pair filter rates reported in Appendix F.4 therefore measure related but non-identical quantities, and may differ on the same SAE.

sections.heading: F.2.1 Per-Architecture L 0 L_{0}
sections.text: The DAME framework partitions features into dominance quantiles based on per-input attribution share. When an SAE has very high L 0 L_{0} (many features active per input), each feature contributes a smaller fraction of the activation magnitude, diluting the dominance signal. Table 7 reports median L 0 L_{0} per architecture in three forms: absolute count, percentage of dictionary size, and percentage of the activation dimension d in d_{\text{in}} of the residual stream. The L 0 / d in L_{0}/d_{\text{in}} column is the most informative diagnostic: a sparse decomposition should have L 0 ≪ d in L_{0}\ll d_{\text{in}} , otherwise the SAE is no longer compressing the activation into a sparse code. Top- k k -based architectures (BatchTopK, TopK, Matryoshka) sit comfortably below 10 % 10\% of d in d_{\text{in}} . PAnneal, Standard ReLU, and JumpReLU range from ∼ 20 \sim 20 – 50 % 50\% . Gated SAEs in our benchmark have median L 0 L_{0} of 126.9 % \mathbf{126.9\%} of d in d_{\text{in}} —they activate more features per input than the residual stream has dimensions. This regime is not a meaningful sparse decomposition: dominance is spread thin across many active features, and the per-feature attribution share that DAME measures is too small to be informative. This explains why the Q1 deficit is not significant for Gated and JumpReLU on real LLMs even though it appears strongly under controlled synthetic sparsity (Appendix D.3.2 ).

The high L 0 L_{0} values reported above (especially for Gated) likely reflect this hyperparameter mismatch rather than an intrinsic architectural property. A proper per-LLM sparsity sweep is left to future work; the synthetic validation (Appendix D.3.2 ) sidesteps this issue by controlling sparsity directly during training. sections.heading: F.2.3 Pairwise Accuracy Results
sections.text: The pairwise accuracy metric (measuring whether the model correctly identifies which of two examples has higher activation) shows similar patterns to perfect ranking accuracy. Across all SAE configurations, Q1 features achieve lower pairwise accuracy than Q2–Q4 features, with the gap varying by architecture and family. The sparsity-pairwise accuracy correlations (included in Table 11 ) show similar weak, inconsistent patterns as the perfect ranking accuracy correlations, with only 4.5% of overall correlations and 6.9% of Q1 correlations reaching statistical significance. However, pairwise accuracy shows a stronger positive correlation pattern for Q1 features (59.8% positive) compared to perfect ranking accuracy, suggesting that sparsity may have a slightly more beneficial effect on Q1 pairwise accuracy.

sections.heading: F.3.1 Three-Metric Composite as Proxy for Monosemanticity
sections.text: Practitioners often use a three-metric composite (dead feature proportion + sparsity + MSE) as an in-training proxy for monosemanticity, since these metrics are computationally tractable compared to full DAME evaluations. This practice is grounded in the superposition hypothesis [ Elhage et al., 2022 ] , though prior work has questioned whether optimizing these proxies yields interpretable features [ Karvonen et al., 2025 , Smith et al., 2025 , Gao et al., 2025 ] . To our knowledge, no prior work has quantitatively validated this relationship. We compute rank correlations between the three-metric composite and DAME monosemanticity scores across all configurations (defined by SAE family, architecture, and width) that appear in both the completeness and DAME evaluations. We find a strong positive correlation with Q1 monosemanticity (Spearman r s = 0.71 r_{s}=0.71 , p < 0.001 p<0.001 ) but only a weak correlation with overall monosemanticity ( r s = 0.36 r_{s}=0.36 , p = 0.012 p=0.012 ). Despite the strong Q1 correlation, top-10 overlap is near-zero (1–2/10).

sections.heading: Implications.
sections.text: The three-metric composite is a reasonable proxy for Q1 monosemanticity, useful when practitioners care primarily about a feature’s strongest activations. For full activation-range monosemanticity or extreme optimization, direct evaluation remains necessary.

sections.heading: Dead-feature pair inflation and filter rates.
sections.text: The within-quartile shares above are reported after filtering out pairs that involve a dead feature (firing count = 0 =0 in the redundancy evaluation sample). The filter only removes within-Q4 pairs. We filter for two reasons. First, a feature that never fires contributes nothing to model computation, so a high decoder-cosine match to such a feature does not represent semantic redundancy. Second, dead features tend to retain decoder directions close to their random initialization, and pairs of features with frozen-init decoder directions can spuriously match each other above the cosine threshold—an artifact of training dynamics, not of true semantic duplication. The unfiltered quantile share for some architectures is therefore dominated by these dead-feature pair counts in Q4, which masks the Q1 effect. Per-architecture pair filter rates and the unfiltered quantile shares are reported in Table 18 : filter rates range from < 1 % <1\% (Gated) to over 50 % 50\% (JumpReLU). The unfiltered shares for BatchTopK, Matryoshka, and JumpReLU place a substantial fraction of pairs in Q4—once dead-feature pairs are removed, the Q1 concentration becomes apparent in every architecture (compare with Table 17 , left). Note in particular Standard ReLU (unfiltered Q1 ≈ \approx Q4 at 38%) and JumpReLU (unfiltered Q4 > > Q1): these two architectures have the highest dead-pair filter rates (38.85% and 51.73%, respectively), so their unfiltered Q4 column is heavily inflated by dead-feature pairs; after filtering, Q1 dominates for both. sections.heading: Architecture-Specific Redundancy Patterns.
sections.text: The comprehensive redundancy analysis across over 600 SAEs from 7 families reveals clear architecture-dependent and model-size-dependent patterns. Standard ReLU shows the highest overall redundancy and the strongest Q1 concentration. This is most severe in smaller models: TinyStories Standard ReLU shows up to 28.6% of Q1 features involved in redundancy, while GPT2-Small shows up to 10.3%. In contrast, larger models ( SAEBench Pythia , SAEBench Gemma ) show much lower Q1 redundancy percentages despite using the same architecture. JumpReLU shows high total redundancy in some configurations but with negative Q1 gaps, indicating redundancy is distributed across quantiles rather than concentrated in Q1. Gated shows intermediate patterns, with moderate redundancy that is less concentrated in Q1 than Standard ReLU. sections.heading: G.3 Per-Input Dominance ( ρ ¯ i \bar{\rho}_{i} )

We use it for stratification because a non-atomic feature occupying a large share of a representation can distort a large portion of the interpretation of that input. Beyond aggregate firing and magnitude statistics, per-input dominance reveals structural patterns where the same small set of features persistently dominates individual input reconstructions. sections.heading: Appendix H Dominant Features: Explanation Analysis
sections.text: This appendix provides a detailed analysis of the text explanations of features, examining linguistic patterns, semantic content, and relationships between explanations for dominant features. Unlike quantitative metrics, explanation text reveals what language models identify as the semantic content of features, offering insights into interpretability patterns.

sections.heading: H.1 Q1 Dominant Features: Explanation Patterns by DAME Score
sections.text: We analyze explanations for Q1 (most dominant) features, comparing those with high versus low DAME scores to understand what makes some dominant features more interpretable than others.

sections.heading: H.1.1 Explanation Characteristics

While word counts are similar (22.1–23.9 words), there are important differences: Q1 low DAME features have the longest explanations (23.9 words, +1.3 vs baseline) despite the lowest DAME scores (0.425, -0.257 vs baseline). In contrast, Q4 high DAME features have the shortest explanations (22.1 words, -0.5 vs baseline) and highest DAME scores (0.862, +0.180 vs baseline). Q1 low DAME explanations more frequently mention XML tags (+34.2% vs baseline), attributes (+24.2%), and domain-specific terms like datatype and minOccurs , indicating a focus on technical markup patterns rather than semantic content. Q4 high DAME explanations emphasize grammatical elements ( indicating , prepositions , conjunctions ), while Q4 low DAME explanations use more generic terms ( related , words , tokens ). sections.heading: H.1.3 Explanation Complexity Patterns

While mean values are similar, the distributions reveal subtle differences: Q1 high DAME features show slightly more consistent specificity scores, while Q1 low DAME features have more variable word counts, suggesting less coherent explanation patterns. Figure 39 : Explanation complexity metrics by category. Metrics are similar across categories, but distributions reveal subtle differences in consistency.

sections.heading: H.2 Domain-Specific Patterns
sections.text: Figure 40 shows domain classification patterns across quantiles. Explanations are classified into domains based on keyword matching: XML (tags, attributes, datatype), punctuation (commas, marks, quotes), structure (sentence, sequence, beginning, end), grammar (conjunction, preposition, verb, noun), and function words (common words like “the”, “and”, “or”, “of”, “to”, “in”). Explanations matching keywords from multiple domains are classified as mixed . Q1 features show a high proportion of “mixed” domain classifications, combining XML, punctuation, structure, grammar, and function word patterns. This mixed nature may contribute to lower average DAME scores: features that combine multiple domain patterns may be harder to interpret coherently. Figure 40 : Domain patterns by quantile. sections.heading: H.3 Discussion
sections.text: Our explanation analysis reveals several important patterns: 1. Explanation length/complexity does not predict interpretability: Q1 high DAME, Q1 low DAME, and Q4 features have similar explanation metrics, suggesting that interpretability differences stem from content rather than form . 2. High DAME Q1 features focus on general linguistic patterns: Explanations emphasize conjunctions, articles, and general structural elements (commas, transitions), suggesting these features capture coherent, generalizable semantic patterns. 3. Low DAME Q1 features focus on domain-specific patterns: Explanations emphasize XML tags, technical markup, and domain-specific structures, suggesting these features capture less generalizable, context-dependent patterns.

sections.heading: Appendix I SAE Geometry: Mean-Direction Clustering and Encoder–Decoder Mismatch
sections.text: This appendix provides detailed geometric analysis supporting our focus on decoder cosine similarity rather than encoder similarity for evaluating non-redundancy. The key insight is that encoder weights function as gating mechanisms that must orient orthogonally to typical activations to satisfy sparsity constraints, while decoder weights define the semantic content written into the residual stream. We present evidence from three complementary geometric analyses: (1) activation space clustering behavior, (2) encoder-decoder-input angular relationships, and (3) learned weight distributions relative to the activation mean direction. Together, these analyses demonstrate that encoder similarity is fundamentally unsuitable for measuring feature redundancy, while decoder cosine similarity captures the semantic relationships that matter for interpretability.

sections.heading: I.1 Activation Space Clustering and Its Implications
sections.text: Transformer activations in high-dimensional spaces exhibit strong clustering behavior around a dominant mean direction. This geometric property has important implications for how encoder weights must be oriented to achieve sparsity. Figure 41 : Surface coverage for 95% of data across all evaluated models. The plot shows median and maximum surface coverage across layers for each model. For comparison, a uniform distribution on a sphere would require 95% surface coverage to contain 95% of the data. Actual activation data requires much smaller surface coverage (typically 1–33%), demonstrating that activations cluster near a dominant mean direction rather than being uniformly distributed. This clustering behavior forces encoder weights to orient nearly orthogonally to the mean direction to achieve sparsity. The clustering phenomenon is consistent across all layers and models we evaluated. Figure 41 shows that even the maximum surface coverage across layers remains well below what would be expected from a uniform distribution. This geometric constraint is fundamental: if activations clustered uniformly on the sphere, encoder weights could point in any direction and still achieve sparsity. Instead, the strong clustering near a mean direction forces encoders to carve out narrow firing regions by orienting nearly orthogonally to this mean. Figure 42 : Distribution of surface coverage values across layers for each model. Each point represents one layer’s surface coverage for 95% of data. Box plots show quartiles, with median values marked. The consistent low surface coverage across all layers and models demonstrates that activation clustering is a universal property of transformer representations, not specific to particular layers or architectures. This geometric structure is what necessitates the orthogonal orientation of encoder weights. Figure 42 shows the distribution of surface coverage values across layers, revealing that the clustering behavior is consistent throughout the network depth. The median surface coverage remains low (typically 5–15%) across all layers, with some variation but no systematic trend toward more uniform distributions in deeper layers. This geometric structure is universal across the models we evaluated, establishing that encoder weights must consistently orient orthogonally to the activation mean direction to satisfy sparsity constraints.

sections.heading: I.2 Encoder-Decoder-Input Angular Relationships
sections.text: The clustering of activations near a mean direction creates systematic angular relationships between encoder weights, decoder weights, and input activations. Understanding these relationships is crucial for understanding why encoder similarity fails as a redundancy metric. Figure 43 : Median angular distances between encoder–decoder, encoder–input, and decoder–input vectors across all SAE families. Encoder–decoder distances range from 24–50 ∘ (median), showing systematic mismatch between encoder and decoder directions. Both encoder–input and decoder–input distances are large (82–88 ∘ ), demonstrating that both encoder and decoder vectors orient nearly orthogonally to typical input activations. The encoder–input distances are typically slightly larger than decoder–input distances, consistent with encoders needing to be more orthogonal to satisfy sparsity constraints. Figure 43 shows the three key angular relationships. The encoder–input mismatch is a constraint imposed by sparsity requirements, while the decoder–input mismatch reflects the semantic diversity of features. This distinction explains why encoder similarity cannot capture redundancy: two features with similar encoders may still encode different concepts if their decoders differ, while two features with different encoders but similar decoders are genuinely redundant.

sections.heading: I.4 Synthesis: Why Decoder Cosine Similarity, Not Encoder Similarity
sections.text: The three analyses presented above provide complementary evidence for why decoder cosine similarity, not encoder similarity, is the appropriate metric for evaluating feature redundancy: From the activation clustering analysis: Activation clustering forces encoder weights to orient orthogonally to the mean direction. This geometric constraint means that encoder directions are primarily determined by sparsity requirements, not semantic content. Two features with similar encoders may have similar firing patterns, but this similarity reflects shared sparsity constraints rather than shared semantic content. From the angular relationship analysis: Encoder–decoder mismatch (24–50 ∘ ) demonstrates that encoders and decoders serve fundamentally different roles. Encoder–input and decoder–input distances are both large (82–88 ∘ ), but for different reasons: encoders must be orthogonal to satisfy sparsity, while decoders encode semantic directions. The systematic difference (encoders typically 1–6 ∘ more orthogonal than decoders) reflects the stronger orthogonality requirement for encoders. From the weight distribution analysis: Both encoder and decoder weights diverge substantially from the activation mean (88–94 ∘ ), but encoders are consistently slightly more orthogonal than decoders. This pattern reflects the different optimization pressures: encoders must satisfy sparsity constraints, while decoders must encode diverse semantic directions. Together, these analyses establish that: 1. Encoder directions are primarily constrained by sparsity requirements, not semantic content. 2. Encoder–decoder mismatch is natural and necessary, reflecting their different roles. 3. Encoder similarity cannot distinguish between features that share sparsity constraints versus features that share semantic content. 4. Decoder cosine similarity directly measures semantic redundancy, which is what matters for interpretability. This geometric understanding supports the formal argument in Section 3 : encoder non-redundancy does not imply decoder non-redundancy (two features can have different encoders but similar decoders, leading to semantic redundancy), while decoder non-redundancy implies encoder non-redundancy (two features with different decoders cannot have identical encoders in an optimal SAE). Therefore, decoder cosine similarity is the appropriate metric for evaluating feature redundancy.

sections.heading: J.1 Controlled Comparison of Per-Feature Scoring Rules
sections.text: We compare per-feature scoring rules in a controlled synthetic setting in which the generator, rather than any evaluator, fixes which explanation is correct. For each of 80 independently generated synthetic features (40 lexical-strength and 40 contextual-strength features), the generator defines a three-level activation rule, H > M > Z H>M>Z . For every feature we construct a matched E exact E_{\text{exact}} explanation that states this relationship and an E reverse E_{\text{reverse}} explanation that preserves the trigger, active support, explanation frame, and comparable length, but reverses only the high-versus-middle relationship ( M > H > Z M>H>Z ). Generator truth therefore fixes E exact > E reverse E_{\text{exact}}>E_{\text{reverse}} before any scorer is queried. This isolates the case in which two scenes have the same binary support but differ in activation strength: both explanations identify the high and middle scenes as active and the zero scene as inactive, but they disagree about which active scene has greater activation. Every scorer receives the same feature, explanation, and held-out evidence. Each feature is evaluated on 18 permutation-balanced held-out H / M / Z H/M/Z triplets, so the scene types do not occupy fixed display positions. Methods are compared only through a common within-feature endpoint: whether the method assigns a higher native held-out score to E exact E_{\text{exact}} than to E reverse E_{\text{reverse}} ; raw scores are not compared across output spaces. The experiment comprises 14,400 requests, all successful, and the inferential unit is the synthetic feature ( N = 80 N=80 ), not an individual request. Figure 49 : Controlled comparison of per-feature scoring rules on 80 synthetic features with generator-fixed ground truth. Bars and the “Strict” column give the number of features whose correct explanation is scored strictly above the reversed one; the tie-credit rate counts a tie as one half. Figure 49 shows that DAME ranks the correct explanation above the reversed one for all 80 features, compared with 67 for discretized magnitude and at most 22 for the binary and fuzz-style methods. Under a family-stratified feature bootstrap, DAME’s tie-credit advantage over discretized magnitude is + 0.11875 +0.11875 (95% interval [ + 0.0625 , + 0.18125 ] [+0.0625,+0.18125] ); its advantages over binary detection, AutoInterp-style binary scoring, and the fuzz adaptation are + 0.41875 +0.41875 , + 0.69375 +0.69375 , and + 0.75625 +0.75625 , respectively, with all intervals excluding zero. The fuzz comparator is our synthetic marked-cue adaptation inspired by Paulo et al. [2024] . The comparison shows the benefit of preserving high-versus-middle activation information rather than collapsing all nonzero activations into one binary class.

sections.heading: J.2 DAME and Binary AutoInterp on the Same Features
sections.text: Prior AutoInterp-style binary assays evaluate features individually and summarize them feature-uniformly; without conditioning on dominance, such an aggregate does not ask whether its errors are concentrated in the small subset of features that carries most of the representation. We test this on two SAEs from the main benchmark with a DAME Q1 deficit, one Gemma and one Pythia, by applying a prior-style binary marked-token AutoInterp assay to the same features. Rather than comparing the two assays’ raw scores, we ask whether each reproduces the Q1-versus-Q2–Q4 gap. DAME shows Q1 deficits of − 11.83 -11.83 pp and − 9.50 -9.50 pp, whereas the binary assay shows + 0.13 +0.13 pp and + 0.35 +0.35 pp. On these two pre-selected SAEs, the dominance-conditioned gap exposed by DAME is not reproduced by the feature-uniform binary assay.

sections.heading: J.6 Held-Out Support Containment
sections.text: We also evaluate held-out support containment on the synthetic benchmark: when a feature fires (its encoded activation is positive), is the same ground-truth variable consistently present? For a ground-truth variable c c , let r c r_{c} denote raw containment, the number of examples on which the feature fires and c c is active divided by the number on which the feature fires, and let p c p_{c} denote the fraction of examples in which c c is active. For each feature we select the variable with the highest corrected score on 25,000 discovery examples and report its score on 25,000 disjoint held-out examples. She starts bending backwards … In Gemma-2-2B, a PAnneal-4k SAE ( trainer_5 ) has features 1352 and 2535 with decoder cosine 0.794 and fresh Jaccard 0.088. sections.heading: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
sections.text: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The abstract and introduction claim three contributions—the atomic interpretable unit framework, the DAME methodology, and the empirical finding that dominant features are systematically less monosemantic and more redundant—each of which is delivered in the corresponding section of the paper. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. • The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. • The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. • It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Yes; we provide a dedicated Limitations appendix (Appendix B ) covering four items: model scale (a small- to medium-model primary benchmark with limited larger-model checks), the conditional rather than absent nature of ground-truth concept sets in real LLMs, the proxy nature of LLM-based monosemanticity scoring (a limitation shared by all auto-interpretability methods, including ours), and hyperparameter-transfer caveats across LLMs. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. • The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper. • The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be. • The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. • The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. • The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. • If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. • While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not include formal theorems or lemmas requiring proofs. The atomic interpretable unit framework and the encoder–decoder asymmetry argument are presented as definitions and conceptual derivations in the main body, not as numbered theoretical results. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results. • All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced. • All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. • The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition. • Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. • Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Yes; Appendix C details the experimental setup, all SAE families and architectures evaluated, and training hyperparameters for our newly trained SAEs, while Appendix D specifies the per-criterion proxy-metric definitions. We also release the evaluation code and result data as supplementary material. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. • If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable. • Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. • While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example (a) If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. (b) If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully. (c) If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset). (d) We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results. 5. Open access to data and code Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Yes; we release a public code repository ( https://github.com/ritengzhang77-max/SAE-AIU ) containing the evaluation framework, training pipeline, and aggregation scripts, alongside per-SAE result data and a README documenting installation and reproduction commands, and the checkpoints of our newly trained SAEs ( https://huggingface.co/ritengzhang/SAE-AIU ). Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code. • Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark). • The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc. • The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why. • At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable). • Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted. 6. Experimental setting/details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Yes; Appendix C lists the training schedule, optimizer settings, activation storage and feature-management hyperparameters, evaluation batches, and per-architecture variants for the SAEs we trained, and credits the SAEBench / jbloom / CanRager release configurations for the externally loaded families. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them. • The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material. 7. Experiment statistical significance Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Yes; the main DAME results (Section 4.1 ) are accompanied by per-SAE Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (computed via scipy.stats.wilcoxon , one-sided, with each SAE as the unit of variability) with reported p p -values and Cohen’s d d effect sizes; the main redundancy results (Section 4.2 ) report endpoint enrichment with 95% SAE-bootstrap confidence intervals; the SAEBench correlation analysis (Appendix D.6 ) reports Spearman ρ \rho ( scipy.stats.spearmanr ) with significance markers, and the decoder–explanation similarity validation (Appendix D.1.1 ) reports both pooled-pair and per-SAE Spearman ρ \rho . Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper. • The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions). • The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.) • The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors). • It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean. • It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified. • For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates). • If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text. 8. Experiments compute resources Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Yes; Appendix C.3.5 reports the GPU type and memory (4 × \times NVIDIA Quadro RTX 6000, 24 GB each), per-SAE training-time range, and approximate total compute budget for both training and evaluation. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage. • The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute. • The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper). 9. Code of ethics Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines ? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Yes; the work is an evaluation methodology for sparse autoencoders, conducted using publicly released models and datasets, and we have reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. The work does not introduce any new dataset, deployed system, or human-subject component. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. • If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics. • The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction). 10. Broader impacts Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Positive impact: our framework and DAME methodology raise the rigor of SAE evaluation, which directly supports interpretability-based safety oversight (circuit tracing, feature attribution, intervention) used in alignment research. Negative impact is minimal: we release an evaluation framework rather than a deployable model or dataset, do not improve any generative or surveillance capability, and use only previously released models and datasets. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed. • If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact. • Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations. • The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster. • The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology. • If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML). 11. Safeguards Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: We do not release any high-risk assets. The paper releases evaluation code, per-SAE result files, and the SAE checkpoints we trained; we do not release new model checkpoints with high misuse potential, and these SAE checkpoints are interpretability artifacts attached to small- to medium-scale models with no demonstrated dual-use risk. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks. • Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters. • Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images. • We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort. 12. Licenses for existing assets Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Yes; Appendix C.3.6 lists each external asset (SAE families, models, datasets, libraries, and the LLM explainer and judge models) with its license, including those for which the public release does not declare an explicit license, and all usage complies with the corresponding terms. We do not redistribute any third-party model weights, SAE checkpoints, or datasets beyond pointers to their original public locations. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets. • The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset. • The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include a URL. • The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset. • For scraped data from a particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided. • If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of a dataset. • For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided. • If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the asset’s creators. 13. New assets Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Yes; the public code release (training pipeline, evaluation framework, aggregation scripts, and sample result data) is documented via a top-level README and per-folder READMEs covering installation, the data layout, and reproduction commands, and the released SAE checkpoints are documented by a model card. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets. • Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc. • The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used. • At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file. 14. Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not involve crowdsourcing or research with human subjects. Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained?
