Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.30474v1 [cs.LG] 21 Oct 2026 Rethinking SAE Evaluation: An Atomic Interpretable Unit Framework Reveals Hidden Polysemanticity and Redundancy Riteng Zhang Affiliation: Purdue University Email: zhan5982@purdue.edu Xiaoqian Wang Affiliation: Purdue University Email: joywang@purdue.edu Abstract Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) were originally motivated by discovering monosemantic features, a property that characterizes individual features but does not specify what the learned feature set should look like as a whole. As SAEs have increasingly been adopted for attribution, circuit discovery, and intervention, researchers have begun evaluating metrics that describe global properties of the feature set, such as sparsity, dead feature rates, reconstruction fidelity, and disentanglement, a diverse set that extends far beyond monosemanticity. However, this implicit shift beyond monosemanticity has not been formalized as a clear, well-defined objective that comes before these evaluation metrics. Without such an objective, existing metrics remain ad hoc, with their necessity unjustified. In this work, we formalize this ultimate objective by introducing a new paradigm for SAE evaluation: requiring that SAE features, and more generally dictionary-based decompositions of model representations, form an atomic interpretable unit basis, a coordinate system for semantically meaningful explanation. Under this paradigm, we organize existing and new measurements such as DAME (Dominance-Aware Monosemanticity Evaluation) as proxy metrics and introduce a comprehensive benchmarking framework. Evaluating hundreds of SAEs across multiple architectures and model families, we uncover failure modes in which some SAEs appear monosemantic under existing evaluation metrics while remaining functionally polysemantic: the most dominant features, those contributing most to model computation, are systematically less interpretable and more redundant. These failure modes warrant attention from SAE researchers as targets for improved training and architectures, and motivate dominance-aware evaluation as a standard check for practitioners before SAE features are deployed for attribution, circuit tracing, or intervention. 1 Introduction Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) entered mechanistic interpretability with a clear and well-motivated objective: addressing superposition by recovering monosemantic features ( Elhage et al., 2022 ) . Superposition arises when neural networks—particularly transformer-based language models—represent more meaningful concepts than they have activation dimensions, forcing multiple concepts to share the same representational space and rendering individual neurons polysemantic ( Elhage et al., 2022 ; Scherlis et al., 2022 ) . SAEs address this challenge by learning an expanded, sparse dictionary of feature directions. Concretely, they decompose a layer’s d in d_{\text{in}} -dimensional activations into m ≫ d in m\gg d_{\text{in}} learned features, with the goal that each feature corresponds to a single interpretable concept. Early work demonstrated that this sparsity-based dictionary learning approach can successfully disentangle superposed representations ( Sharkey et al., 2022 ; Cunningham et al., 2024 ; Bricken et al., 2023 ) , isolating coherent conceptual directions from an otherwise entangled activation space and offering a compelling solution to interpretability in large language models. As SAEs began to be used for LLM attribution, circuit discovery, and intervention ( Templeton et al., 2024 ; Marks et al., 2025 ; O’Neill and Bui, 2024 ) , researchers introduced diverse evaluation metrics: reconstruction fidelity, sparsity levels, dead feature rates, disentanglement, and intervention performance ( Gao et al., 2025 ; Rajamanoharan et al., 2024b ; Chanin et al., 2025 ) . Different works emphasized different subsets ( Bricken et al., 2023 ; Cunningham et al., 2024 ; Gao et al., 2025 ) , while benchmarking efforts like SAEBench ( Karvonen et al., 2025 ) organized them into systematic taxonomies containing eight diverse metrics spanning four capability categories (reconstruction, concept detection, interpretability, and feature disentanglement). Yet a foundational question remains unaddressed: what objective do these metrics collectively serve? When one of these proposed metrics degrades, the SAE is deemed deficient—but the underlying notion of quality remains undefined. Connections between metrics are unclear, and their necessity is justified only post hoc. This gap reflects a deeper issue: monosemanticity, the original objective proposed for SAEs, is insufficient. A feature is monosemantic if it activates on a single coherent concept rather than responding to multiple unrelated patterns. As a local property of individual features, monosemanticity has nothing to do with metrics like reconstruction fidelity or dead feature counts that concern the feature set globally . The proliferation of metrics reveals an implicit shift toward a global objective—but one that remains theoretically unclear and unspecified. Some works have begun to explicitly propose foundational criteria for what properties the feature set itself should possess, such as atomicity, uniqueness, stability, and completeness ( Leask et al., 2025 ; Bussmann et al., 2024b ; Ayonrinde et al., 2024 ) . However, these properties and metrics are typically invoked without justification for why this particular set is necessary and sufficient, and crucially, without first specifying what function SAE features are meant to serve —the underlying objective that would determine which properties matter and why, which in turn determines what metrics should be used to evaluate them. Appendix A provides a more detailed discussion of the history of SAEs and the evolution of SAE evaluation. (a) (b) Figure 1 : (a) Paradigm shift in SAE evaluation: from expecting isolated monosemantic features to requiring that features jointly form an atomic interpretable unit basis. Under the old paradigm, newly proposed metrics function as tweak-and-patch additions, analogous to epicycles. (b) Natural atomic units in vision vs. language. Pixel patches exhibit bounded interpretive ambiguity, while individual tokens are structurally overloaded with unrelated roles. In this work, we address this foundational gap by formalizing a new paradigm for SAE evaluation (Figure 1(a) ). We specify (1) the ultimate objective that SAE features should serve: forming an atomic interpretable unit (AIU) basis (Section 2 )—a coordinate system in which attribution and intervention are semantically meaningful. Under this paradigm, we derive (2) five necessary criteria for interpretable feature dictionaries—non-redundancy, completeness, monosemanticity, no dead units, and per-input sparsity—as direct consequences of the atomic interpretable unit objective (Section 2 ). Building on this theoretical foundation, we develop a comprehensive SAE-specific evaluation framework (Section 3 and Appendix D ) that reorganizes existing measurements and introduces (3) novel metrics—particularly DAME (Dominance-Aware Monosemanticity Evaluation) for assessing monosemanticity, and decoder-based redundancy metrics with theoretical and geometric justification for why non-redundancy should be enforced on decoder directions (Appendix I )—to operationalize these criteria at scale. Our newly proposed metrics expose (4) critical failure modes—SAEs that appear monosemantic under existing metrics while remaining functionally polysemantic due to dominance (a feature’s per-input fraction of total activation; Section 3.1 ) and redundancy (distinct features with near-identical decoder directions; Section 3.3 ) effects previously undetectable by prior evaluation schemes (Section 4 ). Beyond these core contributions, we also: (5) provide a comprehensive open-source benchmark (Appendix F ) across existing SAE families including SAEBench, JBloom, and CanRager, as well as (6) a large suite of newly trained SAE variants spanning multiple architectures and three different LLMs to systematically explore the hyperparameter space. Code is available at https://github.com/ritengzhang77-max/SAE-AIU and the checkpoints of our newly trained SAEs at https://huggingface.co/ritengzhang/SAE-AIU . 2 The Atomic Interpretable Unit Framework Understanding how language models make decisions requires explanations that are both faithful (accurately reflecting internal computation) and human-understandable (expressed in meaningful terms). Modern attribution methods identify which units contribute to predictions, but they do not determine which units are appropriate to explain over . Faithful attribution over the wrong units yields explanations that are computationally faithful yet not meaningfully interpretable to humans. To formalize what makes attribution meaningful, we introduce two key objects: Concepts ( 𝒞 \mathcal{C} ). The set of concepts we want to explain—objects, syntactic roles, semantic relationships, reasoning patterns, and other meaningful computational units that matter for understanding model behavior. Interpretable units ( U U ). The units we actually attribute to during explanation. Each unit u ∈ U u\in U must be interpretable to humans and can relate to one or more concepts in 𝒞 \mathcal{C} . Unlike raw computational elements (individual pixels, tokens, or neuron activations), interpretable units are chosen specifically to support meaningful attribution. Here, an atomic explanatory unit is a basic coordinate to which attribution is assigned directly, without further decomposition within the chosen explanatory interface. 2.1 Why Natural Coordinates Fail: Intuition For natural model coordinates, U U is formed from or composed of basic architectural elements. We can examine whether these natural choices of U U satisfy even the minimum injectivity requirement (Figure 1(b) ). Vision: partial success. For traditional image models that don’t involve complex reasoning steps, we can take U U to be pixel patches. This approximately achieves 𝒞 → U \mathcal{C}\to U injectivity: visual concepts (objects, parts, textures) occupy compact, limited-overlapping spatial regions, so different concepts typically map to different patches. A pixel patch participates in only a few human-meaningful concepts; moreover, spatially coherent patches have bounded interpretive ambiguity . Given a patch that participates in a concept, a human observer can usually identify a small, tightly related set of plausible interpretations—e.g., a dog ear’s shape, color, texture, or the broader category “ear.” These alternatives are few and semantically coherent, so input patches can serve as useful interpretable units for visual attribution, even if they do not correspond perfectly to a single concept. LLMs fail at input level. For language models, the natural choice is U U = token spans. However, tokens simultaneously participate in many unrelated conceptual roles spanning multiple levels of abstraction. Consider the token “Socrates” appearing in the syllogism: “Socrates is human; all humans are mortal; therefore Socrates is mortal.” Attribution to this token cannot distinguish whether the model is responding to its lexical identity, its role as a named entity, its function as a logical variable, its position as the subject of a premise, participation in a syllogistic reasoning pattern, or surface cues such as capitalization or sentence-initial position. These interpretations are not minor variants of the same concept but belong to fundamentally different conceptual categories. As a result, the mapping 𝒞 → U \mathcal{C}\to U is highly non-injective: many unrelated concepts collapse onto the same token, making attribution inherently ambiguous. LLMs fail at activation level. At the activation level, we might take U U to be individual neurons or groups of neurons. However, language models exhibit superposition ( Elhage et al., 2022 ) : they represent far more features than activation dimensions. Each neuron or residual stream coordinate already mixes many unrelated internal features. Because of superposition, 𝒞 → U \mathcal{C}\to U fails injectivity: multiple distinct concepts are superposed onto the same neuron, so neuron-level attribution cannot meaningfully distinguish which concept is active. The minimum requirement revealed. These failures across different choices of U U reveal a fundamental requirement: for attribution to be semantically meaningful, distinct concepts must map to distinct units—formally, the mapping 𝒞 → U \mathcal{C}\to U must be injective. Vision achieves this through spatial locality; LLMs fail because tokens participate in many overlapping concepts and neurons exhibit superposition. Without injectivity, when a unit activates, we cannot tell which concept is responsible, making attribution ambiguous. 2.2 Atomic Interpretable Units via SAEs Sparse autoencoders offer a fundamentally different approach. Given this key distinction—that SAEs explicitly construct U U to approximate 𝒞 \mathcal{C} —the goal for SAE features is not merely to function as an atomic interpretable unit basis, but to directly learn features that approximate a meaningful concept set. This requires two conditions: each feature represents one concept ⇒ \Rightarrow monosemanticity (C3): features shouldn’t mix unrelated concepts; and each concept has one feature ⇒ \Rightarrow non-redundancy (C1): features shouldn’t duplicate representations. The granularity problem. Even with one-to-one correspondence, the SAE must learn features at the right level of detail. Let m m denote the number of learned features and let n ideal n_{\mathrm{ideal}} denote the appropriate number of concepts for this layer. These conditions are necessary rather than sufficient for causal use, which additionally depends on whether and how features are recruited by downstream layers’ computation under a particular context, intervention, and outcome. However, these criteria were derived at the conceptual level---describing what properties the feature set must satisfy---without specifying how to operationalize them as concrete measurements in the SAE context. 1 1 1 Many existing SAE evaluation metrics act as joint proxies for multiple criteria out of the five; a detailed correlation study and per-evaluation mapping (covering Sparse Probing, SCR, TPP, Feature Absorption, RAVEL, and Unlearning from SAEBench ( Karvonen et al., 2025 ) ) is provided in Appendix D.6 . For C2 (Completeness) , C4 (No dead units) , and C5 (Per-input sparsity) , certain standard proxy metrics from prior work map naturally to our framework: for example, reconstruction fidelity metrics for completeness; firing frequency statistics for dead units; and mean L 0 L_{0} (the number of features active on an input) for sparsity. We adopt these established measurements in our benchmarking with one addition: an effective sparsity metric that accounts for activation magnitude distribution (detailed in Appendix D ). 3.1 The Local-to-Global Aggregation Problem for C1/C3 The remaining two criteria— C1 (Non-redundancy) and C3 (Monosemanticity) —present a qualitatively different measurement challenge. Unlike C2/C4/C5 , which admit direct dictionary-level proxy measurements , C1/C3 are defined as local properties : monosemanticity is a property of individual features, while non-redundancy is a property of feature pairs. Consequently, determining whether an SAE satisfies C1/C3 as global requirements for an atomic interpretable unit basis demands an explicit local-to-global aggregation principle . Yet most existing SAE evaluations effectively assume one by default: they aggregate local measurements across features (or feature pairs) using uniform weighting to produce a single dictionary-level score. This assumption is fragile because feature usage is highly imbalanced: a small subset of units accounts for a disproportionate share of activation (and therefore attribution), and thus disproportionately influences SAE-based interpretability analyses (e.g., circuit tracing); their quality should therefore be weighted more heavily. When a non-atomic feature accounts for a large share of a representation, misinterpreting it distorts a large portion of what the SAE represents at that input. This raises a fundamental open question: whether increasing sparsity constraints truly decompose features into finer-grained atomic units, or instead primarily reduce sparsity loss by suppressing non-dominant features while concentrating computation into a smaller set of increasingly dominant ones. 3.2 C3: Monosemanticity—DAME Monosemanticity concerns whether inputs with sufficiently large activation (e.g., { x : | f i ​ ( x ) | ≥ ϵ } \{x:|f_{i}(x)|\geq\epsilon\} ) share a coherent semantic property. In practice, this is assessed using the standard auto-interpretability pipeline ( Bills et al., 2023 ) , which proceeds in two stages. First, for each feature i i , an LLM (the explainer ) is shown a small set of high activation examples and produces a natural-language explanation describing the feature’s firing behavior. Second, the proposed explanation is evaluated on held-out validation inputs S i S_{i} using an LLM-based judge: the judge predicts the feature’s activation behavior, with labels derived from the precomputed activations f i ​ ( x ) f_{i}(x) for x ∈ S i x\in S_{i} . Validation framing. Prior approaches frame validation in ways that fail to test whether explanations can distinguish high from low activation, particularly under severe feature firing frequency imbalance. Binary classification asks whether a feature fired or not ( Paulo et al., 2024 ) . However, if a rare feature never receives a positive example during validation, the explanation cannot be tested at all. For instance, suppose a polysemantic feature i i truly activates on two unrelated but rare triggers—mentions of Socrates and mentions of Los Angeles —so that f i ​ ( x ) > 0 f_{i}(x)>0 on only ∼ \sim 0.01% of tokens. If S i S_{i} is sampled uniformly at random from the corpus, it is likely that no input in S i S_{i} contains either trigger, yielding an all-negative validation set. In that case, any explanation (even an incorrect one that only describes “Socrates” and ignores “Los Angeles”) will appear to achieve perfect accuracy simply by always predicting “does not fire.” The same issue applies symmetrically to high-frequency features: when a feature fires nearly 100% of the time, negative examples become impossible to sample, so false positives cannot be detected. Discretized magnitude prediction bins activations into fixed intervals (e.g., 10 bins) normalized by each feature’s maximum activation ( Bills et al., 2023 ) . This remains problematic: when features exhibit outliers, the maximum activation skews the bin boundaries, compressing inputs with meaningfully different activation magnitudes into the same label. Important distinctions go untested. DAME. We propose Dominance-Aware Monosemanticity Evaluation (DAME), which addresses both challenges: 1. Dominance-stratified feature sampling. To address the dominance weighting problem, we rank features by mean dominance ρ ¯ i \bar{\rho}_{i} and sample from each dominance quantile separately, ensuring evaluation coverage across the full dominance spectrum. Dominance is used for stratified sampling and aggregation; it is not an input to any feature’s score. 2. Activation-balanced contrastive validation. For each feature, we bin all inputs into three groups (low, medium, high activation) based on that feature’s own activation distribution using quantile splits. Each validation question presents one example from each bin, without showing activation values, and asks the LLM to rank the three examples by activation strength given only the explanation, guaranteeing adaptive coverage across the full activation spectrum within every validation question. We score each feature by perfect ranking accuracy : the fraction of validation questions for which the LLM predicts the exact activation order (Appendix D.3.1 ). In a controlled test of high-versus-middle activation reversals that preserve binary firing support, DAME ranks the correct explanation above the reversed one for all 80 synthetic features, compared with 67 for discretized magnitude and at most 22 for binary/fuzz-style scoring (Appendix J.1 ). 3.3 C1: Non-Redundancy—Decoder Cosine Similarity Non-redundancy requires that distinct features encode distinct concepts. Though not often evaluated, when researchers do measure redundancy ( Karvonen et al., 2025 ) , they use decoder cosine similarity, sim ​ ( i , j ) = d i ⋅ d j ‖ d i ‖ ​ ‖ d j ‖ \text{sim}(i,j)=\frac{d_{i}\cdot d_{j}}{\|d_{i}\|\|d_{j}\|} . However, this decoder-side measure is adopted without explaining why decoder redundancy (rather than encoder redundancy) is the appropriate notion for C1. We provide a justification below and report per-quantile decoder cosine similarity in Section 4 . Encoder-decoder asymmetry. Each encoder weight vector w i w_{i} (the i i -th row of W W ) functions as a sparse classifier that carves out a small firing region in activation space. Because of the per-input sparsity constraint, most features must fire on only a tiny fraction of inputs. However, transformer activations cluster near a dominant mean direction (Appendix Figure 41 ), causing encoder weights to be almost orthogonal to this mean (typically near 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} ; Appendix Figure 46 ). If w i w_{i} were close to the mean input direction (say, within 40 ∘ 40^{\circ} ), the feature would activate on nearly all inputs, violating sparsity. Thus encoder directions cannot reliably align with semantic features. This encoder–decoder angular mismatch is natural and benign (Appendix Figure 43 ): the encoder w i w_{i} specifies a decision boundary that controls when a feature fires, while the decoder d i d_{i} specifies the concept—the semantic direction it writes. Sparsity eliminates encoder redundancy. Moreover, sparsity constraints already regulate encoder-side redundancy. If two features have w i ≈ w j w_{i}\approx w_{j} , they fire on the same inputs with the same magnitude, so the SAE can merge them into a single feature with decoder d i + d j d_{i}+d_{j} , achieving identical reconstruction while reducing the sparsity penalty. Decoder redundancy, however, is not directly penalized by the standard SAE objective (reconstruction plus sparsity), and can therefore persist. Empirical validation of the proxy. We use feature sharding to describe a pairwise representational pattern in which features share (nearly) the same decoder direction d i ≈ d j d_{i}\approx d_{j} , have dissimilar encoders w i ≉ w j w_{i}\not\approx w_{j} , and fire on complementary regions of activation space while writing the same semantic direction. Feature sharding can preserve reconstruction fidelity and per-input sparsity while reducing dead features, and may therefore be favored by objectives with explicit dead-feature penalties. An SAE can thus appear healthy under common diagnostics even as its effective semantic dictionary collapses to far fewer directions. Concretely, consider a semantic direction encoding the concept of color . Rather than learning a single feature that activates whenever color is relevant, an SAE may shard this direction into multiple features whose encoders gate activation on additional, unrelated contextual factors (e.g., gendered language, syntactic role, or discourse position), effectively learning features of the form color ∧ \wedge context . During attribution, whenever color contributes to the model’s computation, exactly one such shard fires—maintaining sparsity—so attribution is tied to the shard’s gating context rather than to the underlying concept of color itself. A functional sharding example. Their encoder and decoder cosine similarities are 0.2066 and 0.7405, respectively. Together, the separated natural supports and aligned intervention effects provide a functional sharding case: the two features specialize to different determiner contexts while producing similar downstream decoder writes. Sharding differs from feature absorption ( Chanin et al., 2025 ) , in which a general-concept feature fails to activate on more specific cases while other features take over its role; the two can coexist. In terms of firing positions, sharding corresponds to decoder-aligned features that fire at largely separate positions, whereas absorption is compatible with one feature’s firing positions being largely contained within the other’s.
